That on and after Monday, November 14, 1949, until the end of the present session, the house shall meet at 11 o'clock in the morning of each sitting day, and that in addition to the usual intermission at 6 o'clock p.m., there shall be an intermission every day from 1 to 3 o'clock p.m.
He said: The reason for presenting this motion at this time is my understanding that it is the hope of a large number of members of the house that it will be possible to complete the work of this session not later than December 3. Of course no one would wish to slight the consideration that still must be given to the matters that remain to be dealt with. By going on the eight-hour day schedule at this time we feel that it will be possible to give due consideration not only to the matters which are already indicated on the order paper, but to some which are yet to be introduced.
As you will see, Mr. Speaker, there are twenty-three items under government orders at the present time, and some of them have several subdivisions. For instance, there are the estimates, which will provide the occasion for the debate on external affairs which the Minister of Public Works announced it was our hope to initiate next Wednesday. There are the estimates of other departments in which the general item of administration has not yet been considered, and these will give rise to some debate.
In addition to those measures and such others as are on the order paper of the other place, it is the intention of the government to introduce a certain number of additional bills, of which I have a list here.
There will be a bill to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. It is not a substantial amendment; it is designed to clarify and to make more readily workable certain of the provisions of the act. There will be a bill to fix
the duration of the Agricultural Prices Support Act, and another to fix the duration of the Fisheries Prices Support Act. A bill will be introduced to amend the Customs Tariff Act, in certain minor particulars having to do with articles which under the tariff are now prohibited entry. There will be a bill to amend the Industrial Development Bank Act, to enlarge the proportion of the available funds that can be used in what are classified under the act as the larger loans. Certain minor amendments are required to the Dominion-Provincial Tax Rental Agreements Act to conform with the legislation and practices of certain of the provinces.
The Department of Trade and Commerce will have a bill to amend the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act, and also a bill to provide assistance in the production of coal in the maritime region of Canada. The Department of Transport will have a bill to increase the amount of stores that may be kept as a bank to supply the requirements of the services. The present act has a limitation that is found to be insufficient to allow the department to have a bank of stores necessary for convenient administration.
There is also to be a bill dealing with the encouragement of construction of Canadian vessels. That will be brought down at an early day.
In addition to these, there will come from the Senate, or at least it is hoped that there will, the consolidated national defence act, which is now under consideration in that house; a bill to amend the Customs Act, and a bill to amend the Surplus Crown Assets Act, clarifying the procedure for the disposal of surplus property of the various departments of government. These bills are being introduced in the Senate, probably at its next sitting.
Hon. members will recall that the speech from the throne refers to a bill to provide for the continuance of functions now vested in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. After careful consideration it is proposed to introduce, before the end of the session, legislation to provide for the redistribution of the functions of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply and the Department of Mines and Resources among three new departments, to come into effect upon proclamation. The departments are to be known respectively as the Department

of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Department of Resources and Development, and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration; under the latter will be placed the administration of Indian affairs. Though this is really one subject three bills will be required, and a consequential amendment to the Salaries Act.
Within the next few days the Minister of Finance expects to make in the house the statement which he promised to make before the end of the session, in regard to the government's policy as to crown property in the municipalities. Consequential upon that statement, which will require for its implementation legislation that it is intended to introduce not this session but early in the next session, some legislation may be required, probably in the form of an additional supplementary estimate, to bridge over the period until the permanent legislation is enacted.
I would not like hon. members to feel that we were definitely committing ourselves that there will be nothing else. Nothing else is now foreseen, but additional legislation may be required because of unforeseen developments between now and the end of the session. But hon. members will realize that this is still quite an important program, particularly when added to the program we have before us on the order paper. If it is felt that the public interest is being properly served by our proceeding at the pace we have adopted since the beginning of the session, there will be opportunity for full and serious consideration of all these matters. But it would not be possible, or certainly not as easy, to feel that satisfaction about it if we did not add these two additional hours to each day's sitting between Monday and the time at which it is hoped prorogation can take place.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxlon (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: CORRESPONDENCE WITH RESPECT TO PRICE FIXING AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, hon. members will have it in mind that today is Remembrance day, the thirty-first anniversary of the armistice which ended the great war of 1914-18. Today we remember reverently the service and the sacrifice of the men and women who gave their lives in the defence of their country and their freedom. The Memorial chamber in the peace tower lists their names and tells the story beginning with this inscription on the walls:
Read how free men. throughout this land kept faith in the hour of trial and in the day of battle, remembering the traditions they had) been taught, counting life nothing without liberty.
Today we are reminded of the events that led up to the second world war, and of the effort in lives and money and materials that was needed before we could win the victory and continue free. We learned again that


eternal vigilance is the price of freedom. Unfortunately the hope for peace and security with which we ended the second world war has not been fulfilled. The Soviet union has turned its back on the co-operation that helped to bring victory against the axis powers. Instead of world partnership for peace, in which all nations could work constructively to improve human relations and conditions, we have a limited partnership with the non-aggressive half of a divided world, and are forced to devote much of our energy to the negative but necessary task of preventing war.
While circumstances force us to take greater measures than we have ever taken before in peacetime in order to make our contribution toward the means of preventing an outbreak of war, we must remember that we have further objectives. We have no warlike intentions. Our objectives are peace and conditions of security in which we can work for the better life we know is possible, both for ourselves and for other nations. We seek the security of all, and of the good that this condition can bring. As a means to this end we must do our utmost to prevent war. Our defence activities are a means to prevent war. They are an essential means necessary to our preservation as a nation.
The ceremony that took place today and our thoughts at this time will strengthen us in the conviction that those we remember at this moment were right to "count life nothing without liberty", and that we are right in doing whatever is necessary to guard what they preserved.
To assist in understanding our defence needs, and to save the time of the house which an extended statement would take, I caused to be prepared and made available a statement on our national defence which I now table. This statement is intended to give:
(1)	An account of the present international situation;
(2)	An appreciation of the defence needs of Canada;
(3)	An analysis of the department's estimates, and
(4)	An account of the various aspects of the work of the department and services.
This should be read in conjunction with the annual report of the department for the year ended March 31, 1949. The annual report is in a new form, giving a much fuller account of activities. Usually it is made available only in February, at the commencement of each session, which means it is almost a year in arrears; but this year we tried to have it available at the commencement of this session, and it was tabled on October 19, some four months earlier than usual. This material is

presented and made available to hon. members because of the importance of national defence.
The international situation makes defence a matter of major government policy. The estimate of $375 million, taken with the supplementary of $8 million, means that we are now spending on defence 16-4 per cent of the national budget, or $28.37 for each man, woman and child in Canada. At present exchange rates, this is considerably less per capita than is being spent in the United States or the United Kingdom, but it is more than is being spent by any other country in the British commonwealth except the United Kingdom, or by any party to the North Atlantic treaty except the United States, the United Kingdom and The Netherlands, all of which have world-wide or extensive colonial interests. The sum now sought represents what the government believes to be the right amount to be spent on defence by Canada in the present fiscal year.
The statement which has been issued deals at some length with the international situation, upon which our defence policy is based. This may be summarized as follows:
1.	The only possible aggressor is the Soviet union.
2.	Any war would be a world war involving all western peoples who would be fighting for their survival as nations and their freedom as men.
3.	The best way to prevent such a war is to confront the forces of communism with such strength as to deter them from attack.
4.	To provide such strength requires the co-operative efforts of the western nations, including the United States and Canada.
5.	Consequently Canada welcomed the North Atlantic treaty as supplementing the United Nations, and, pending the strengthening of the United Nations, as an organization for world-wide security.
6.	Since an attack on Canada could only be made by air or by sea, emphasis must be placed on defence forces; by air-radar stations and communications, backed by interceptors and a relatively small mobile brigade group; by sea-anti-submarine and anti-mine vessels for protection of shipping and coastal waters.
7.	The best place to defeat the enemy is as far away from Canada as possible, and our forces should also serve as the nucleus for the development of our maximum potential.
In the statement you will see an explanation of the considerations which must enter into the preparation of any defence budget. There is also an indication of the costs of some of the equipment used by modern defence forces. I think hon. members will be astonished at the cost of some of the
Supply-National Defence equipment which is mentioned on page 19 of the report. For instance, a Packet transport aircraft of the C-119 type would cost well over half a million dollars. A 5-25 anti-aircraft gun, equipped and installed, would cost in the neighbourhood of $600,000. An antisubmarine vessel of the type of which we have three now on order in Canada would cost $8 million. An airfield equipped with the necessary runways and construction to be used by interceptors would cost from $15 million to $20 million.
As the report emphasizes, the dollar spent on defence is just like every other dollar. It is not rubber; it cannot be stretched. If, as we can show, the amount of some $383 million is needed to meet the requirements of our defence forces this year, then it is perfectly obvious that we can only increase the size of the forces, the equipment or the amount of construction by taking more of the national budget. Planning defences in this country, as in every other country, becomes inevitably a question of assessment of risks and appraisal of priorities.
At the present time more than half of the defence appropriation is spent on personnel-officers, men and civilians-for pay, allowances, pensions, food, clothing, services, and other payments that vary directly with the size of the forces. This amount is as large as it is for two reasons. In the first place, we have tried to create conditions of service which would attract Canadians of ability and character as well as good physique. As to conditions of service, I am sure you will be glad to hear that Canada stands second only to the United States. There the new pay schedules are higher than ours, but other conditions, including pensions, clothing, food, and married quarters, are generally comparable to those in the United States.
The large proportion of the defence expenditure applicable to personnel reflects also the number of men in the armed forces. We have 45,000 in the active forces, another 45,000 in the reserve forces, and 24,000 civilians principally working in dockyards and shops at prevailing rates, making altogether a total of 114,000, of whom 69,000 are employed full time. This makes the department the largest in point of numbers in the government service, and it has, I am led to believe, the widest ramification and the greatest variety of problems.
In the statement and annual report there is a summary of recruiting results, giving figures of enlistments and discharges, and showing the net gain against the establishments fixed for each of the services. During the twelve months ending with September we have taken a total of 12,267 into the active forces, with 4,006 releases, making a
1664	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence net increase of 8,261, or 688 per month. At the present time the navy is up to strength in other ranks, and at the present rates it is estimated that the present ceilings for the army will be reached by September, 1950, and for the air force by December of the same year.
What is most satisfactory is that the rates of release are considerably less than estimated, and that on the termination of the first three years' engagement in the army more than ninety-seven per cent of men are reengaging, and the three per cent who are not re-engaged includes a number who are released as not considered suitable.
During the same period we have taken in 1,523 with the reserve navy, making a net increase of 610. The twenty-one naval reserve divisions have a total strength of 3,468, and the ten air force auxiliary squadrons have a strength of 3,086, which is regarded as making satisfactory progress. The army reserve has a total strength of 38,572, and I feel that a desirable immediate target would be another 10,000. In addition there are 936 in the university naval training division, 2,619 in the university corps of the Canadian officers' training corps, and 679 in the air force university plans, as well as 282 at the Canadian service colleges. We are continuing campaigns to maintain the flow of recruits.
During this period there has been continuous progress in training with active and reserve forces, with emphasis on the training of officers, noncommissioned officers and tradesmen. There are now four plans in effect for the training of officers, with over 5,000 young men taking qualifying courses, a larger number in proportion to population than I believe will be found training to such standards in any other part of the world. We are obtaining good results form the service colleges, university plans, and the local command contingent arrangements. Further developments and changes will be made to meet needs as they arise. Consideration is being given to changing arrangements for the training of executive officers for the navy.
One of the greatest shortages in meeting an emergency would be skilled tradesmen, large numbers of whom are required in modern forces. Fortunately the ordinary young Canadian, whether he be bred on the farm or in the towns or cities, has great aptitude for work of this type. However, we are adopting various means of increasing trades training in the active and reserve forces, and also have developed an interesting plan for training cadets from vocational schools. We have been discussing with representa-
[Mr. Claxton.l

tives of industry ways and means of adding to the numbers of men skilled in all essential trades.
The services today are large-scale educational institutions, running the gamut from post-graduate schools, such as the national defence college for senior officers and civilian officials, to nursery schools operated cooperatively by service personnel at isolated centres. The navy is operating specialist schools on both coasts in a total of twelve branches. The army has schools for each of the fourteen corps at nine different camps. The R.C.A.F. has eight schools at six different stations. We operate sixteen schools for over 2,000 children of service personnel at isolated centres. This year a total of over 1,200 senior officers are taking courses at command schools. Every active and reserve unit and camp has a number of classes.
In all this, as in everything else, there is close co-operation with the United States and with the United Kingdom. Indeed, our relations are closer than ever before-closer I believe than have ever existed between the forces of any other countries.
The figures before you will show that in X 948-49 a total of $145 million was spent on supplies, equipment, construction and the like, covered by over 65,000 contracts placed through Canadian Commercial Corporation. Major items of equipment purchased include aircraft, ships, electronic and electrical instruments, motor vehicles and construction. Let me say a word about each of these main items.
Aircraft: Good progress is being made with the development of the Canadian-designed XC-100 aircraft, which will be test-flown this year. The development of this aircraft was commenced in 1946, and in each of the last two years we have put in two years of work, which has enabled it to be brought to this stage of development several years sooner than is usually the case in the peacetime development of a new type. The aircraft was entirely designed in Canada to suit Canadian conditions, and if it flies according to its planned characteristics it will be a very useful jet aircraft. Under licence from the United States manufacturer we have placed an order for one hundred F-86 planes, to be manufactured by Canadair Limited. We are continuing to overhaul and modify other aircraft. During 1948-49 we spent $22 million on aircraft. This year I expect the figure will be $45 million.
Ships: The next largest single item in our planned program of development is ships for the navy, largely related to antisubmarine work. We have placed orders for a transport

icebreaker, three new high speed antisubmarine vessels largely of Canadian design, four minesweepers, and a gate vessel, costing about $40 million.
Electronic and electrical equipment: All three services use large quantities of radar and other electronic and electrical equipment. We have a large scale program of production of the most modern and high-powered equipment by Canadian firms. The amount provided for electronic and communications equipment in this year's estimates is $19 million.
Motor vehicles: In the modern army there is one motor vehicle for every four men. The three services today have in use or in reserve in the neighbourhood of 20,000 personnel and load carrying vehicles. Many of these require replacement, and all require care and maintenance. For this purpose we are spending this year some $10 million.
Construction and maintenance of buildings: The largest single item on the material side of the activities of the services is for the construction and maintenance of buildings. Every building we have in good condition is being used, and we have under way a large-scale building program of married quarters. At the beginning of 1947 we had 1,100. When this year's construction program is completed we should have over 7,300, representing a very substantial contribution toward meeting the housing shortage. This year Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is constructing a large number of dwellings earmarked for the use of service personnel. Altogether this year there has been allocated for construction and maintenance of buildings for defence purposes in these estimates and by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation a total of $91 million, comparing with the peak figure on defence construction for 1942 of $219 million.
These figures are supplemented in the annual report and the statement, which have been made available. It occurred to me that in a brief enumeration I could best put before hon. members some of the other matters which may be of interest either by way of report or of program, and after doing this I shall be glad to answer any questions I can. By way of concise report, during the period under review I may mention that-
1.	The ration scale has been improved as to quantity and variety, and also provides for supplementary cash payments in certain cases, thus bringing our ration scale up to anything there is anywhere.
Supply-National Defence
2.	Clothing has been greatly improved, both as to quantity and quality, as far as possible on a uniform basis for all three services.
3.	We have made continued progress in the erection of married quarters, and commenced the construction of new barrack accommodation for single men.
4.	A shipbuilding program has been set under way with an Arctic icebreaker and development orders for three new design antisubmarine vessels, four minesweepers and a gate vessel.
5.	We have pressed on with continued progress on the all-weather fighter, the order for 100 F-86's, the modernization and overhaul of other planes; opened three new air force establishments, including interceptor squadrons at St. Hubert and Chatham, and the navigation school at Summerside.
6.	We have a large electronic program.
7.	We have reopened Royal Military College and established Royal Roads on a triservice basis.
8.	There has been an increased program of sea training for active and reserve naval forces, the first visit by Canadian naval vessels to Hudson bay, as well as the reactivation of H.M.C.S. Cornwallis for training new entries.
9.	The training of the army brigade group has been pressed on, with extra attention to airborne and Arctic fighting and further improvements in summer and winter training arrangements.
10.	The period under review has seen the continued development of co-operative arrangements with the United Kingdom and the United States, highlighted by the visits of the late Hon. James Forrestal and Hon. Louis Johnson, Secretary of Defence of the United States, Right Hon. Arthur Henderson, Secretary of State for Air of the United Kingdom, and numerous other distinguished visitors, and return visits by myself to Washington, with frequent exchanges of officers at every level.
11.	Major General F. F. Worthington was appointed co-ordinator of civil defence.
12.	The industrial defence board and the defence medical and dental advisory board have been set up.
13.	The department has assumed responsibility for inspection, formerly vested in the inspection board.
14.	Medical services were reorganized to take advantage of D.V.A. facilities.
15.	Fire fighter services were established, and fire and accident prevention campaigns carried out.

Supply-National Defence
16.	We have continued the campaign for support in recruiting, with the desired results in every respect except for the reserve army.
17.	The security arrangements have been strengthened.
18.	The services have assisted in meeting civilian needs in fire fighting and search and rescue operations.
19.	We have set up a system of tri-service communications across Canada.
These are some of the achievements. On the debit side we have:
1.	Two regrettable losses of planes of the R.C.A.F., both apparently due to bad weather.
2.	Regrettable losses of flyers and aircraft of H.M.C.S. Magnificent.
3.	Disciplinary troubles in the R.C.N., due in part to the difficulties of post-war adjustment.
4.	Adverse press reports on Exercise Eagle, which I believe were due principally to our failure to explain the nature, objects and possibilities of the exercise.
Looking toward the future, in addition to carrying on the program I have outlined I emphasize the need for-
1.	Improved arrangements for training in Canada for naval executive officers, and further improved arrangements for qualifying officers for the R.C.N. from the universities.
2.	Improved arrangements for in-service education and trades training.
3.	Continuous examination of establishments, military and civil, to promote economy and efficiency.
4.	Increased efforts to inform and enlist the support of the civilian community.
In these remarks I have necessarily only touched the highlights of a large scale combined operation. I say it is a combined operation, for I believe the officers and men of our three services are working loyally as a team in the service of their country. During the past two and a half years this has not been a particularly light task or an easy period. Though this particular job imposes heavy and exacting administrative responsibilities requiring continuous attention at headquarters, I have felt that it also required the knowledge and interest resulting from visits to the units across Canada, and I must say I have found these stimulating and inspiring. I have said before and repeat that there is nothing second-rate about the officers and men of our armed forces. It is a privilege I value highly to work with them.
The efforts of Canadians in two great wars have demonstrated our capacity to make a great contribution to the defence of our country and to the common cause of freedom. In proportion to population, no country contributed more to restore those peaceful conditions abroad on which our own prosperity
[Mr. Claxton.J

so largely depends at home. Our representatives earned respect for Canada as a nation standing for justice in international dealings, just as our soldiers, sailors and airmen earned respect for Canada by their competence, their courage and their conduct. Today and in the future Canada's defence organization must ensure the integrity of our territory and meet any obligation we may assume under the North Atlantic treaty.
Towards this end I shall welcome informed and constructive criticism and every kind of assistance, and I believe in this we shall have the support of all hon. members and of all the people from end to end of Canada.

speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that hon. members of this house will appreciate the statement which has been tabled this afternoon by the Minister of National Defence, and which explains in considerable detail, as he said, the policy governing the organization, training and operation of our defence forces. But I find it difficult to reconcile with that action the last statement he made. Just before he sat down he said he would welcome informed criticism of the policy of his department in order to build better defence forces for Canada. Every hon. member in this committee wants to see our defence forces-the navy, the army and the air force-the finest that this country can possibly produce. But I suggest that the tabling at this time of a statement outlining that policy is of no help whatsoever to this committee. We have not had an opportunity to study the contents of the statement; therefore we cannot give that type of informed criticism which the minister has expressed a desire to receive by way of assistance in the development of our armed forces. I do not know how long this debate will go on, but I hope that it will go on long enough, or that it will be adjourned at some time during the discussion of these estimates, and resumed later in order that we may have an opportunity to read the statement that the minister has today tabled.
The minister referred to the fact that today is Remembrance day. I cannot help feeling that it is a strange, sad, ironical circumstance that we should be discussing estimates for national defence within a few hours of the time when members of this house and hundreds of thousands of people all across Canada were standing in reverent memory of the sacrifices which had been made by Canadians in past wars. I feel sure that it was the fervent prayer of all those who attended these ceremonies that the sacrifices made by Canadians in the past would not have to be repeated.
The extent of the attendance at these memorial services can perhaps be emphasized

by recalling the fact of the differences in time throughout Canada. I look at the clock, and I realize that the parade in my own village on Vancouver island will just now be dispersing. I do not think it is an exaggeration to say that, at every hour during the twenty-four, men in some part of the world, with their wives and children, will be standing in front of a cenotaph and praying that there may not be another repetition of the catastrophes of the past.
With vivid memories of the sacrifices that those men have made, I cannot but turn my thoughts back to the policies which have enabled Canada, during the past century and a half, to preserve herself and to help to maintain the freedom of this world.
At the beginning of the nineteenth century Canada was threatened by a series of international disturbances. It was then the settled policy of the United Kingdom government to station Jn Canada regular forces of the British army, equal in number to the regular forces then maintained by the only enemy which was anticipated at that moment, namely, the United States. Those British regular regiments were stationed in small garrisons at nodal points from the Atlantic to the great lakes. In some cases the garrisons were not strong, merely manning forts, but they were a deterrent or a stopgap which enabled the citizens of Canada, when the emergency developed, to rally behind those regular regiments and, after a period of training and equipping, to fight nobly in the defence of this country. The essential point I make here is that regular units were available in order to gain the time for the civilian soldiers to become ready.
As we pass over the years-we need not bother about the South African campaign, because we hardly took a great part in it- we find that in 1914, around those militia units which then existed, the citizens of Canada rallied, as they also did in 1939. In the winter of 1914 the units which had made the greatest progress in their development went over to England, and in the spring of 1915 they took part in some of the great battles of that campaign. But, remember, there had been other troops who had drawn to themselves the first onslaught of the enemy's attack. The British regular army should have been decimated and should have perished in gaining that time. That is immaterial, but it is a fact. Time was gained by their heroic withdrawal from Mons and the first battle of Ypres and so forth.
Then came 1939, and again around our nonpermanent and permanent force units the citizens of Canada rallied. Again, after a period of training, those who had made the
Supply-National Defence most progress in that respect were transported across to the United Kingdom, and there in the United Kingdom they underwent a further period of training, a further period of equipping. In the meantime other troops from other countries were holding off the enemy while that period of training went on. I remember very vividly how, in the spring of 1940, the first Canadian division moved out from Aldershot. It was a circus. It was a circus as we rattled our way with indentured vehicles up to Midlands, there to occupy another position. Our training went on, and as the battle of Britain was being fought after Dunkirk and the danger became greater in September, 1940, one year after the outbreak of war the first Canadian division was rehearsing at dawn day after day a counter-invasion role. As their commander I know that I stood up and said to battalion after battalion: "I know that you will fight gallantly but the cost will be heavy because you will not fight skilfully. You are not well trained".
We were fortunate that it was impossible for Hitler's armies to cross that small channel. The air force held them back. The air force attacked them while they were mustering in France in preparation for that invasion.
Again I want to emphasize the fact that while under the system which had held good and had proved itself worthy for the defence of Canada for a hundred and fifty years somebody else had gained the time before the militia of Canada were ready to carry out the magnificent role which brought the crowning victories in these campaigns. Are times changing now? Only a few days ago in this city a great statesman from the United Kingdom said that the card had been played for the last time. I refer to Mr. Bevin's statement in speaking to the Canadian Club here in Ottawa. The card had been played for the last time. What card? The card of gaining enough time to develop your forces for the outbreak of war.
General Crerar, who was in command of the Canadian army during the campaigns in this war, has repeatedly pointed out that if a country is not ready when war breaks out again it will never have a chance to save itself.
The policy which has just been enunciated by the minister, the policy which is described in the annual report of his department, and the policy, as far as I could gather which has been published in the statement that he has just tabled, indicates that this country is relying upon exactly the same policy which has stood this country in good stead for a hundred and fifty years, but which, according to men such as Mr. Bevin and General

Supply-National Defence Crerar, is now out of date. This is the policy as enunciated in the annual report for the Canadian navy:
To provide a well-trained nucleus equipped with ships of the classes needed for coastal defence and the protection of trade, to train reserves and to provide the administration and training personnel and equipment to permit whatever expansion may be necessary.
I now turn to the policy as defined for the Canadian army:
To have in active service a highly trained and mobile force, capable at the same time of defending our territory against any possible sudden attack and also of forming a compact framework around which reserve forces may quickly be built up in case of emergency.
So far as the air force is concerned the policy is as follows:
. . . the R.C.A.F. is to build up and maintain an air strength adequate to meet any immediate attack and to form a nucleus for the formation of larger forces if necessary.
Hon. members will see that at the present time the emphasis is being placed continually on the small compact units. They are relying upon there being a period of time in which the reserve forces of the army, navy and air force may be built up.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that there is much uncertainty, much consternation amongst the people of this country, particularly those people who have had service experience -and there is a very high percentage of our people who have had service experience. There is much uncertainty as to whether this course of relying upon the ability to build up reserve formations, the militia, call it by whatever name you like, when the emergency comes, and relying upon some other forces to gain that time, is a sound policy under present conditions.
In the last few days, or the last few months, an investigation has been carried out by three distinguished men. I refer to the commission set up under Admiral Mainguy to inquire into conditions in the navy. He stated quite frankly that his commission did not make an exhaustive inquiry into Canada's naval policy and the part our navy might be called upon to play in case this country were once again involved in war.
They would have had this annual report of the Department of National Defence before them; and he goes on to say that the knowledge they had did influence them in their inquiry and thought, and the recommendations they submitted. At page 52 of the report the commission states:
There Is a widespread feeling that the available manpower and material have been stretched too far and too thin to meet the requirements of a fighting, convoying and anti-submarine force.
[Mr. Pearkes.3
The report goes on to say that they recommend that the naval complement should be reviewed. In other words, they recommend that we should cut our coat according to the cloth we have, that we should review the whole of our naval policy with regard to the number of ships and men we can maintain and the roles we should carry out.
The report continues at page 42 to state that the comparatively heavy commitments of the navy have required constant operation and hurried change, with the result that training has not gone ahead as fast or as systematically as it should have. The present actual complement of officers and men was stated by several witnesses to be inadequate for the existing commitment.
There are other references to the same question of naval policy. The report drives home the fact that our resources are too thin and have been stretched too far to do all the tasks they are being called upon to do. I do venture to suggest that the same sort of thing applies in respect of the other services -that our resources are being stretched too far and they are too thin to be able to provide these mobile forces and to provide the nucleus for expansion which it is suggested will have to take place under certain circumstances.
I think the expansion which is so essential will be most acutely felt in so far as the Royal Canadian Air Force is concerned. Hon. members will recollect that in the early days of the battle of Britain, in the first years of the war, appalling casualties were suffered among fighter pilots. Replacements were very heavy for fighter pilots, aircraftmen, bomber pilots, bomber gunners-in fact anyone who was in the air. That was where the heaviest strain came. That was where there was almost a breaking point in the battle of Britain. Everyone there at the time has spoken of the glorious action of those R.A.F. and R.C.A.F. pilots who, worn out and exhausted, returned to the attack time and time again against the Germans who were endeavouring to bring the United Kingdom to heel through action of their bombers.
What is the condition regarding the strength of our reserve forces in so far as the R.C.A.F. is concerned? I ask that because it was to the auxiliary squadrons that Canada and the other nations had to look for their supply of pilots. In this connection I take my figures as they appear in table 3 at page 82 of the report of the Department of National Defence. At this point the reserve strength as at March 31 of this year for the reserve army is 36,311. The strength of air crews and ground crews of the reserve auxiliary air force is only 1,427. I heard the figures the minister gave today, which indicated an

increase from that number. I would point out that that increase consists of recruits, because on March 31 they were not there.
I turn next to the training section in the annual report, and at section 18 on page 10 I find that in the Canadian universities there is a enrolment of 2,040 cadet officers training with the officers training corps. In section 20 we see the number of university students training as cadet officers in the R.C.A.F. These would be the personnel who would be first called upon to replace casualties suffered in an air war. What do we find? As against 2,040 army officer cadets there are 366 students in the R.C.A.F. auxiliary.
Surely we are not putting the emphasis in the right place in providing reserves and the expansion which is so essential. Surely we must be realistic. As the minister said, if there is an attack against this country it must come by air or by water. If it comes by air or by water the policy he enunciated, that it must be met as far away from Canada as possible, is the correct policy. To do that we must have a strong air force. We must be able to bring to bear not a small active force supported merely by some 300 students now in training. I suggest that if we are again to rely upon the expansion of essential forces we have to place emphasis where it is most needed in order to carry out the policy announced by the minister of meeting the enemy as far away from Canada as possible. That is not what is being done under the present policy.
Looking at the estimates for this year I find that the details on page 198 show that $8,939,000 is being provided for army reserves. Then when I turn to see what is being provided for the auxiliary of the Royal Canadian Air Force I find that only $3,600,000 is in the estimates, a little more than one-third and less than one-half of the previous amount. The next junior branch is the Royal Canadian Air Cadets, those keen youngsters who are seen occasionally in the high schools across the country. They are allotted $363,000 as compared with $1,002,000 for the army cadets. Again I say that if we are relying upon the expansion of the essential arm, we are not giving encouragement where it should be given. The annual report shows that of the money allocated last year for the R.C.A.F. squadrons and training plan and R.C.A.F. reserves, only $1,067,000 was expended.
I do not want to labour that point any longer. In the light of the statements which have been made by Mr. Bevin, by General Crerar, in the Mainguy report and by many other government officials, I think that there is cause for anxiety and criticism as to whether the policy which has stood us so
Supply-National Defence well over the last 150 years is the correct policy under the very changed conditions which exist in the world today.
I am not in position to say how that can be corrected.
The minister has suggested that he would like the co-operation of every hon. member in this house. We in this party have suggested from time to time a way in which we think he could get that co-operation. We have suggested that if a committee was set up to deal with questions of defence we would be better informed and therefore would be able to give him the advice which he has asked us today to supply. Whether that is the right course, whether that is the course the government is prepared to follow, only the minister can say. But he has asked us for co-operation and that is our suggestion.
I am quite certain that every hon. member shares his pride in the forces of Canada, particularly at seeing these young men come and stand around the cenotaph side by side with the veterans of two past wars. So many of these services remind me of the wonderful poem by Colonel McCrae, the theme of which was that with failing hands they passed on the torch to future generations. I do not believe that it was the meaning of Colonel McCrae, nor is it the interpretation placed upon that poem by the people of Canada, that they were passing on a fiery cross to call the clansmen on some foray. I think he meant that they were passing on a beacon which it was hoped would light the way to better conditions in the world of the future.
As we all know, and as the minister has said, the high hopes of San Francisco, where the United Nations was formed, have not been fulfilled in their entirety. However, I have confidence in the peoples of this world and I believe that ultimately we shall be able to find some other means of settling international difficulties. The time has not yet come when we do not have to maintain strong and adequate armed forces. We want to be able to grasp that torch with strong and firm hands, not with weak and faltering hands.
I believe the people of Canada are prepared to advance these immense sums of money in the hope that the armed forces of Canada will be able to prevent a third world war, in the hope that the armed forces of Canada will be designed to prevent a third world war rather than to win the victory during the later stages of that war, should it come. The people of Canada are making great sacrifices. I admire the minister for not mincing matters when he spoke about the

Supply-National Defence amount of money he was asking the people of Canada to contribute for the maintenance of these forces.
The people of Canada want to know that that money is being spent in the right direction; that the policy the department is following will achieve the ends desired and that we are not merely providing this money to maintain old traditions; that we are not pouring that money into the Department of National Defence only to find that what is to be provided is a useless, futile type of defence if we are ever called upon to fight again. I have grave doubts as to whether the policy being followed by this government is going to achieve the results that Canada expects.

maintopic: CORRESPONDENCE WITH RESPECT TO PRICE FIXING AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is rather significant that on Armistice day we are discussing the estimates for the Department of National Defence. We look back over the last thirty-one years and realize that on November 11, 1918, a sigh of relief went up from everyone in Canada, and indeed across the world, because one great war had ended; we look back and realize that now we have seen a second and even greater world war; and yet today we are forced by circumstances to discuss defence once again, and the possibilities of entering another world-wide struggle. I do not think any member of the house can do other than support the defence estimates that have been presented to us. Of course the tragedy is that after two great wars we are forced to consider anew methods of defence.
Let us not forget that defence lies not only in the strength of our armed forces and the instruments of war that we may build, but also in the condition of our people and the conditions of people all over the world. A short time ago we listened to a very great man speaking in this chamber, Prime Minister Nehru of India. If we followed his address closely we saw that the lesson to be gained from it was that, not in armed strength but in the removal of evil social and economic conditions, the peace of the world really lies. Until we have removed the economic and social conditions that cause unrest and make for war, we have to consider ways and means of national defence in another field. In the ultimate, the manner in which we can best serve our generation, and generations to come, the manner in which we can best bring universal peace to the world, is to seek the security of all mankind economically and socially as well as in every other way.
I hope we have learned another lesson since the last war ended. It is that we must press forward to bring about understanding among the nations of the world in order to prevent


war. From what I have heard said by some of the greatest scientists engaged in the production of atomic energy and the atomic bomb, and from what I have read in their articles and those of military men as well, there is really no adequate defence against modern instruments of war. If we allow war to come upon the world again then the civilization that we know will fall in ruins.
It is not often I agree with spokesmen for the Soviet union at the United Nations or elsewhere, but I read a short time ago that, in the celebration of their national holiday commemorating the revolution of 1917, their national spokesman on that occasion predicted that if war came to the world, as he put it, the capitalist society would be destroyed utterly. I would go further than that and say that civilization of every sort, whether it be capitalist, socialist or communist, will be destroyed utterly in the event of another world war. There is really no defence against modern instruments of war, but of course some reliance can be placed, as the hon. member who has just taken his seat implied, upon negotiation among the nations based upon strength. Consequently if other nations are engaged in strengthening their defensive machinery, lacking collective security we also have to participate in a similar policy.
I am glad that the Minister of National Defence saw fit yesterday to place in the hands of at least some of the members of the house the document I have before me, "Canada's Defence Program". I am sorry that it was received rather late last evening, because I should like to have given closer study to it. As a matter of fact, except for the short time I was in the house last night, I spent the evening reading it, and a very interesting document it is. It indicates the tremendous amount of money that we are going to spend this year on the various projects the minister has enumerated this afternoon. There is the figure of $375 million in the main estimates plus $8 million in the supplementary estimates, a total of $383 million. If you add another $150 million to that you come pretty close to the amount of our total national budget for all purposes prior to the last war. As I say, if you add $150 million to the $383 million, you come close to the total national expenditure of Canada in 1939 and prior years. Sixteen per cent of our country's revenue, $38 per head of our population-

Twenty-eight dollars per head of our population is an enormous

expenditure in a country such as Canada which has so many resources awaiting development. In the autumn of 1946 I had the privilege of being one of the Canadian delegation at the United Nations. Our delegation, through the mouth of the then Secretary of State for External Affairs, the present Prime Minister, placed that point of view forcibly before the general assembly of the United Nations. He urged the necessity of carrying out the parts of the United Nations charter having to do with collective security of the nations in order, as he put it, that we might proceed in a country like Canada to raise the standards of life of the people. Today we have to face an expenditure of $28 per head of population, not for the development of our great resources, not for the raising of our standards of living and the improvement of the lot of our people, but for preparations for defence.
We supported the North Atlantic pact because we believe it is essential under the conditions that exist today, but let me point out that the North Atlantic agreement is a second best only, and that if we are going to have real world-wide security then we must have it on the basis of the United Nations. Consequently we believe that at this time the manner in which we co-operate with others will mitigate to some extent the obligation we have to assume for defence. The minister said in the course of his remarks that the best way to deter the forces of communism was to face them with overwhelming strength. Again may I say, as I said of the Atlantic treaty, in my opinion that is indeed a second best. Perhaps it is the alternative we must accept today, but in my opinion the best way to defeat communism, or what we call communism, is to raise the standards of living of people everywhere, and to see to it that nations are engaged in promoting social justice everywhere. That is the only real and effective weapon against communism; there is no other. Indeed, that was the lesson brought to us in this chamber a few short weeks ago by Nehru.
But since there is not social justice across the world, since there is grave danger of conflict among the nations, then we must guard our own country well; and that means we must consider proposals such as those which have been placed before us this afternoon. The minister told us Canada's forces were merely a nucleus in the event of war, a nucleus of army, a nucleus of navy and a nucleus of air force. While that was criticized by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), perhaps after all that is about as far as we can go if we are to maintain our national economy, and indeed it is as far as most other countries are going at the
Supply-National Defence present time. That is so in the United States, though their forces are many times the size of ours and their expenditures much greater. In the United Kingdom, where they are closer to that part of the world where conflict might arise, the same policy is being followed. Because side by side with the arming of our forces and the organization of navies, armies and air forces, we must maintain our industrial and economic strength; for in the final analysis it is upon our industrial and economic strength that victory or defeat will depend.
And let me say in considering the arming of our forces, whether they be naval, military or air force, I believe that this should be done, as I have so often said in the house, without profit to any group or individual in this land. We of this movement have always stood for the nationalization of the main munition industry. It may be argued that many industries not recognized today as munition industries are of importance in wartime and that therefore a policy such as I have suggested could not be carried out. But there are certain vital industries manufacturing the equipment of war that should be in the hands of the Canadian people through public ownership. I regretted very much the sale of Canadair two or three years ago, because I foresaw that in the event of a program such as the minister has laid before us today this industry would be vital in the realm of national defence; and so it is proving to be. And if I may say so, while I believe the company is operating efficiently, I was disturbed to see that it was sold to the Electric Boat Company. Anyone who knows the story of that company between the two wars I think will agree with me; or anyone who has read the book on the munition industry, entitled "The Private Manufacture of Armaments", written a few years ago by a gentleman who was here within the last two or three weeks, Right Hon. Noel-Baker, will recall that in this book the exposure of the anti-social operations of that company is quite complete. So I say we believe that the main armament industry of the country should not be a matter of private profit for any corporation or any individual, but should be a national project under complete national ownership. During the last war we saw in our own country how great, nation-wide industries were strengthened and enabled to attain an even more monopolistic position in our society than they had previously: Aluminium Limited, Canadian Industries Limited, and now Canadair. That is one feature of the defence program with which we disagree, the manner in which the instruments of war are being provided for our army, navy and air force. We believe that

Supply-National Defence should be undertaken as some of these projects were undertaken during the war with efficiency. We can point with great pride in this country, I think, to some of the industries which operated under the Department of Munitions and Supply as crown companies owned by this nation.
Then we agree that the conditions affecting the personnel of the armed forces should be the very best. I have read the naval report to which reference was made this afternoon, and one of the criticisms it expresses is the distance which was maintained between the officers and men. I think the authors of that report were quite correct when they said the average young man entering the Canadian navy was somewhat different to the average young man entering the British navy. In the past at least the officers of the British navy have been drawn from a different class than the men serving in the lower ranks. That is not the case in our own country, where officers and men have obtained their education often from the same schools, and have come from the same sort of homes with the same environment. Consequently the sort of discipline one finds in the British and some other navies should not be applied in the Canadian navy. So I congratulate the minister on having said, as he did, that steps would be taken to more particularly Canadianize our navy. That does not mean merely painting maple leaves on the funnels of the ships. It means much more than that: the organization of a navy based on Canadian conceptions and Canadian conditions, with a Canadian atmosphere among officers and men. Discipline there must be; but I have always believed, both in my own lifework and generally, that the best kind of discipline is one of confidence, rather than a discipline of remoteness or fear. So I am glad indeed to hear that the minister is proceeding with the Canadian-ization of our navy.
He said, too, that it was essential to attract men of good physique. Well, that is essential, but first of all we must raise the men of good physique, and in order to get them we must have a well-fed, well-housed and healthy population. I sat in this house on another November day in 1941 when the then Minister of National War Services, Hon. J. T. Thorson, speaking from a place not far from where the minister is sitting now, read a report of the experience during the first year of recruiting, 1939-40. The house was shocked to learn that some 46 per cent of the young men who had offered themselves for enlistment for overseas service were turned down because of physical defects of one sort or another.


That, it seems to me, was a commentary upon the conditions which had existed for a number of years and which were particularly acute between 1930 and 1939. If we are going to have defence and are going to rely on men and women for that defence, we must see to it that the children of this nation are well housed, well clothed, well fed and-if I may add one other requirement-well educated as well. I therefore say that our defence expenditures should be matched by expenditures for social services and for the wellbeing of the nation generally.
A moment ago I mentioned the fact that education was also an arm of defence, and that statement was never truer than it is today. During the last war we learned the importance of the scientist, the educated technologist and others who possessed above average educational attainments and abilities. Indeed, in spite of those terrible years-and in a way perhaps because of them

in the early days of the war Canada provided the Royal Air Force with a high percentage of pilots and navigators. This was possible because in this country we had a group of young men who had received a high-school education or better. Consequently, when we discuss defence, we cannot forget that it means more than the placing of men in uniform and the building of the machines of war. It means education, especially scientific education, preparation for research and technical activities.
A few moments ago I mentioned the Canadianization of the Canadian navy. In this document I was glad to see that attempts are being made to educate our young men along democratic lines so that in the days to come they may take their places in more responsible positions. One other thing I noticed was the large number of civilians now employed in armed forces activities; they are civilians who are skilled in various lines of endeavour, such as artisans and so on. Let me emphasize once again that just as we need skilled men in the armed services, so we need skilled men and women in industry. I think that most hon. members in this chamber-at least those who were here at the time-will recollect that we had great difficulty, in the first two years of the last war, in equipping the men who were in the armed forces; that we had great difficulty in getting the necessary plans and blueprints for the building of the necessary equipment; and that we had considerable difficulty in getting the necessary skilled labour to make the equipment according to the plans and specifications which we had secured. We should therefore be thinking not only in terms of army, navy and air force, but in terms of building up in our own country a civilian corps of men and women consisting of arti-

sans, technologists as well as scientists, who are so skilled that, in the event of new machines of war being needed if war comes again, which God forbid, they will be able to provide us with those machines in a short time.
To some extent, of course, that objective is being accomplished through the re-education of our veterans, through our technical schools and the scientific research organizations in our universities, and through such projects as the one at Chalk River which some of us are looking forward to seeing next week.
If we look at a list of the scientific advances and changes that have been made since the last war ended, we realize that in a discussion of this sort we cannot think of a future war in terms of the last war or the war before. When we faced the last crisis in the world and in this country, one of the difficulties was that most of us had been thinking in terms of the war of 1914-18, when all of sudden we were faced with an entirely new set of circumstances. Then army, navy, air force and parliament had to unlearn much of what they had learned, between the two wars, out of the lessons of the first one. Because of these new instruments of war that the minister listed, the cost of national defence today is comparatively fabulous. When the minister was speaking, he mentioned "construction" in the estimates amounting to $91 million. That is something that is necessary, and I am not criticizing it; but I did a rough calculation. For the $91 million we could have built
18.000	houses at $5,000 each if we could have been relieved of expenditures of this description. As I say, I am not criticizing that expenditure of $91 million. But when the words "construction for the armed forces" were used, the thought flashed through my mind that if we had been able to use that $91 million for construction for domestic needs, this year we could have constructed
18.000	additional houses with a value of $5,000 each.
Once again I want to say that while we support the measures that the government consider necessary-and after all, the government must make this decision; they have information that we do not possess-and while we support these defence proposals, we believe that every effort must be made by our Department of External Affairs, supported by the people of this country, to endeavour to bring about international understanding so that such expenditures will be unnecessary in the days to come, and so that we may have real collective security through international organization. When we get that we, in common with other nations, shall be 45781-1064
Supply-National Defence able to embark upon a program of international and national disarmament and shall be able to use the vast amounts of money nations now expend in this way for the benefit of the people of all countries.
The minister paid a tribute, as did the hon. member for Nanaimo, to the young men and women who served in the last war. Distinctly I remember really believing thirty-one years ago, as I did for some years, that the world had had a blood bath that it would not forget, and that the little children growing up in our homes in 1918, as my own son was, would not be called upon to face another such war. Well, they were called upon to face that war. It seems to me that one of the obligations that parliaments have, that the Department of External Affairs has and men and women of good will everywhere have, is to do our level best to see that the world is so organized, the standards of living are so raised and the causes of discontent so removed that the generation of little boys and girls growing up in our homes today, and in some instances our grandchildren, will not be called upon to do what our sons and daughters were called upon to do.
I admired the young men and women in the Canadian armed forces when I had the privilege of going overseas in 1941 and again in 1944. The hon. member for Cape Breton South, the hon. member for Melfort and I were privileged in September 1944 to visit our armed forces in Belgium, which had just been occupied. Anyone who met Belgian citizens at that time and heard the tributes that were paid to the young Canadians who had occupied that country will never forget it. They were well liked because of their courtesy and of their general behaviour. We felt very proud of these young men and women, but I hope that we may never have to send overseas contingents of young men and women to do the same kind of job that they did.
While we have that hope we cannot neglect to do all we can to promote the defence of our own country, lest some calamity befall this nation and the world. Therefore, what I want to say is that while we support these defence expenditures made necessary by the uncertain international situation, we want to say to the house that we believe the best way to defeat subversive elements, communism, if you wish to call it that, in our own country and throughout the world, is to do everything in our power, both in our own country and in co-operation with all nations, to raise the standards of living and to remove the causes of poverty, misery and want, out of which future wars are likely to arise. With these words I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that we must support the estimates presented by the government.

speechtext:
Up to
the present time the debate has been enlightening and in the main enjoyable. The hon. member who has just taken his seat has voiced the sentiments of almost everyone in this chamber as regards the ideals we are working for. With his expression of ideals I have no quarrel at all. To them I say, Amen. But when it comes to means whereby these ideals may be achieved then I take sharp issue with his proposals.
All during world war II it was declared by government spokesmen everywhere that what is physically possible shall be made financially possible. In the main during the war that promise was honoured. With the coming of the peace the same principle ought to have been applied in an effort to win the peace. I find myself completely amazed to discover that not one single spokesman for the government, or anyone from the opposition, has insisted that we should make what is physically possible financially possible in our endeavours to win the peace. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that if these particular people whom I have mentioned had been as industrious, as determined, to make what is physically possible financially possible in their endeavours to win the peace, we should not now be in such necessity to prepare for the greatest war of all times. They apparently forgot the principle that what is physically possible can be made financially possible as regards the peace not only within the nation but among the nations.
Little attention indeed is given to Canada's physical possibilities by the members of the government's side of the house, and I fear by even the members of the Progressive Conservative party. Little attention is given Canada's physical possibilities when we confront problems such as the housing problem of Canada, the transportation problem of Canada, both as regards freight rates and the construction of highways, the price control problem of Canada, including the cost of living; old age pensions, and war veterans' allowances. It never seems to dawn on anyone in these august bodies that what we can do for old age pensioners depends in the last analysis on the food, clothing and shelter we can produce in Canada.
Today the minister has declared in effect that if we Canadians cannot financially afford a safely adequate program of defence, then we cannot have that adequate program of defence, regardless of what may or may not be Canada's physical possibilities. I suppose it will not dawn on the minister and his colleagues that what is physically possible can be made financially possible in preparation for war until we are again in war, when it is
[Mr. Coldwell.i

too late to make what we all would hope might have been a really adequate preparation.
The coming war, Mr. Chairman, will be characterized by lightning speed, transcendent military strategy, designed to paralyse us immediately, unscrupulous surprise, equal to that of Pearl Harbor, and dismaying fifth-column activities, co-operating with the foe.
Bearing this in mind, there are four questions that the minister ought to answer. I do not care whether he does it on the floor of the house or not. But he ought to answer them when he gets back in conference with the able assistants of his department and with his colleagues in cabinet. First: Could Canada fight successfully if the United States were paralysed by strikes or internal disorders? I do not know that I have heard this question even entertained. Second: Is our military industry decentralized appropriately? Third: Have we regional organization for the production and distribution of food, clothing and shelter in Canada in respect of both storing and producing, with respect to providing hospitalization, government, defence, aggression? Have we provision for guerrilla warfare?
I was over in Britain in 1941 with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I was a member of the delegation of the empire parliamentary association in that tragic year of Britain's history. I was impressed with the fact that they had organized Britain into twelve distinct regions. The general idea was that each of those regions was provided with all the equipment such as I have referred to that would enable it to carry on a successful fight against the foe alone. So that if eleven of the twelve regions of Britain were overrun, the twelfth could still shout defiance at the foe, and make good its defiance. I should think it would be the barest fundamental of wisdom in Canada for us to have at least several regions comparable with those in Britain. I doubt very much however that we have any such organization, although it would seem to me necessary.
I am afraid that if by successful manoeuvring a foe could gain control of certain parts of Ontario and Quebec, you could roll down the curtains on Canada. That would be something to be very sorry about, but something for which the Liberal government in Canada would have to assume responsibility, by reason of its policy of centralizing industry during the long years of its regime in Canada.
Fourth: Have we a nucleus and skeleton organization, in respect of personnel, buildings and equipment, for a British commonwealth air training scheme? I am a bit surprised we have not heard about such an air training scheme, especially in the light of

the fact that this scheme played so potent a part in the ultimate victory of our arms in world war II.
Having said this much about the general situation, may I turn to the document called "Canada's Defence Program" which was distributed by the minister among the leaders of the parties, and from which document he quoted rather generously this afternoon. I am sorry it did not reach my hands until 11.15 last night, and that I have not been able to give it as much attention as I should like to have given to so important a document. Nevertheless, under the circumstances, we shall do what we can.
I turn to the second division of it which deals with the international situation, and should like to read into Hansard certain excerpts from that part of the document, commenting upon certain of them. In paragraph 5 on page 6 I find this:
We appreciated that the road to peace was a long and arduous one and that with other members we should have to assume continuous responsibilities for the building and maintenance of peace.
"The building and maintenance of peace" -very well said; but not much done about it. Then, following that-
The people of Canada, through their representatives in parliament, clearly indicated that they were prepared to accept these responsibilities.
They did; no blame on the people of Canada. And from the same paragraph:
No substantial progress has so far been made through the institutions of the United Nations.
And the question ought to be asked, in capital letters of red, and underlined: Why? Everyone will blame the wrong person, just as nearly everyone blamed the wrong person for the outbreak of world war II.
Then I should like to quote from paragraph 7-and I shall not comment at great length, but shall reserve my comments for later. It states-
By the terms of the treaty- and the reference is to the Atlantic pact-
-the parties undertake "to settle any international dispute in which they may be involved by peaceful means," and "to contribute toward the further development of peaceful and friendly international relations by strengthening their free institutions."
As I recall it, the United States signed that document and thus committed herself to the treaty. I should like to ask any citizen of the United States who by chance happened to come in contact with this speech, and I would ask any other person in Canada the same question: What would United States reaction be if the European nations asked for the privilege of introducing the imperial preference system in accordance with their opinion as to how far those preferences would
Supply-National Defence help? I wonder if there would be on the part of the United States a willingness to confer with others in an effort to grant European nations their request? I go on:
-to "encourage economic collaboration"-
I wonder what has been done to encourage economic collaboration, in the realistic sense. We are discussing the international situation. I quote again from paragraph 7:
"The parties separately and jointly, by means of continuous and effective self-help and mutual aid, will maintain and develop their individual and collective capacity to resist armed attack."
I wonder if they have gone as far as mutually helping to raise each other's standard of living, or if they all have fallen back into cutthroat competition-which everyone knows is commercial warfare and leads inevitably to military warfare. It continues:
The parties agree to "consult together whenever, in the opinion of any of them, the territorial integrity, political independence or security of any of the parties is threatened."
I wonder if Canada and the United States have really got right down to grass roots in the endeavour to find out how to raise their respective standards of living so as to prevent the inroads of communism from becoming greater? If they have not, it will not do much good for the minister to get up here and use unctuous phrases in Canada about peace.
Then turn to paragraph 8:
The purpose of the North Atlantic treaty is to establish the joint strength of the democratic countries and, by making aggression clearly unprofitable, give the western nations the opportunity to combat communism, not in the field of war, but in the field of ideas, of practical living and of peace.
I should like to ask, for the benefit of the minister and his colleagues, and especially the Prime Minister, what greater opportunity Canada and the United States could possibly have than they have had given them in order to accomplish this laudable objective.
But we see no results from it. Vast numbers of the people of Canada are living right on the verge of poverty. When the announcement was made that rents would rise it was a calamity to most of them. They do not have much of a margin to go on, and to keep them away from communism, or cushion them against the wily arguments of communists, do they?
Then, turning to paragraph 12 on page 8:
By pooling resources, the effect of the pact should be to reduce the total expenditures which each of the twelve countries would have found necessary for their security had there been no pact. However, that result is some distance off and in the meantime, Canada will have to make such modifications of her plans as may be found necessary to meet the situation.
