Supply-National Defence
I wonder if Canada is making modifications in her plans so as to meet her internal economic and financial situation? I have my doubts.
And then at paragraph 16 on page 9, quoting General Bradley:
"The more I work on our plans lor defence, the more I am convinced that war is not inevitable-
I agree with the gentleman.
-and that our defence plans can be part of a strategy for a lasting peace."
And then on the following page:
War is not impossible . . . but I believe it is unlikely. I believe it can be made increasingly unlikely by our own behaviour-
I agree with that-"our own" behaviour. -if only the American people can adhere to a wise and steadfast course of conduct through the years.
Change "American" to "Canadian" and I would agree with him there also.
There is no absolute security in the world today. But there is relative security, and a way to make that relative security stronger.
Especially in Canada and the United States.
Once we have established reasonable defensive forces, in combination with our friends of the Atlantic pact, the likelihood of an attack against us will be slight.
It surely will be.
X mean (by reasonable defensive forces) forces of such strength that any potential enemy must recognize (a) that it would be foolhardy for him to start a war against us, and (b) that it would be foolhardy for us to start a war against him. I believe that such an equilibrium of forces can be established, and held stable through the years until more civilized long-range solutions can be found.
Those words of General Bradley contain some jewels of wisdom, but I am afraid he did not have in mind the kind of thing that really needs to be done by both nations.
Are Canada and the United States really doing all they can to contribute to and encourage amicable collaboration? I immediately recall the United States' unconditional most-favoured-nations clause that forced Japan into world war II, and probably forced Germany to declare war in the beginning. What about the non-discrimination principle that has practically throttled every nation on the earth today? What about the convertibility of currency fallacy, that ghastly misconception brought about by the Bretton Woods agreement? What about the coerced reduction of imperial preferences which made the lot of Great Britain and the British commonwealth so much more difficult than it otherwise would have been? Those were all embodied or implied in the Bretton Woods agreement and the Minister of National Defence, along with all his colleagues, supported that agreement. I suppose he still
(Mr. Blackmore.]

supports it. That was one of the most pernicious documents ever perpetrated on earth by man. The Geneva and Havana trade agreements were built around the same fallacious principles, and those principles have never been disavowed. I maintain that until those principles are disavowed there is no hope for peace in the world.
May I refer to some of the things that are going on in the world and especially in our neighbouring nation where people are getting up and uttering high-sounding phrases just like those the minister has used. I do not want to be unkind to the minister because I know he is in the hands of a certain group of people who are working toward certain objectives. But he has been one of the leaders in that group, judging by his remarks in this house in times past.
We read in the Christian Science Monitor of November 7 that the government of the United States is limiting the production of many products at the very time when a billion people in the world lack the very things of which she is going to limit the production. Can we speak of that as being a measure designed to produce peace in the world? They are suggesting a reduction in the production of corn, wheat, cotton, rice, potatoes, peanuts, tobacco, citrus fruits and milk in some cities. That is being done at a time when there are tens of thousands of people in the United States not receiving the nourishment they ought to receive.
On November 2 the Christian Science Monitor speaks about the proposed reduction in the production of corn and says that the acreage will be reduced in 1950 to the lowest figure since 1892, that next year perhaps 10,000,000 acres less will be in production than in 1949. That brings up the question: How many commodities in Canada is the government limiting the production of? Not a few! In doing that I contend that their policy is directly contrary to all the high-sounding and pious phrases that appear in the Atlantic pact.
On November 3 Philip Noel-Baker, speaking before the Canadian Club in Quebec, said that one billion people in the world suffer from hunger but that with modern methods world food production could be doubled. Why is not the world doubling it? Until the modern world does that, particularly the United States and Canada, how can we stand here and say that Canada and the United States are doing all they can to prevent the coming of another war? If we cannot be honest, we should at least refrain from talking.
On the financial page of the Christian Science Monitor of October 24, 1949, there

is reference to the Hirsch report. These are specialists in grain; they state that the world need for United States wheat is still vast.
Let us bear in mind something which is vital to this matter we are now discussing. In 1947 the United States sold $11 billion to $12 billion more goods to the world than she bought from the world, and a large proportion of those goods were rather forced on the world. That unbalance was just as great in 1948.
Can anyone maintain that the United States, which is refusing to distribute goods within her own borders so that her own people can buy them, which is refusing to distribute purchasing power, can anyone for a moment argue or even pretend that that nation-this applies equally to Canada-is endeavouring to remove the cause of a coming war? I have been arguing this kind of thing for a long time; hon. members cannot say that they have not been warned about this.
I do not want to be hard on hon. members but I can start and go in any direction and point out that all hon. members except Social Crediters almost broke their silly necks in a scramble to accept the Bretton Woods agreement. Apparently they thought that by accepting that pernicious thing all the evils of the world would be solved and the millennium introduced immediately. With the brilliant men that were in parliament in those days, one would think that they could have seen through the thing. The Social Crediters could.
In 1945 I stood here during the Bretton Woods debate and strove with all the force I had to get the Liberal party to realize the awful step they were taking. At that time a body of about 60 men who sat right over there kept up a noise like a stampede of bulls so that it was impossible for anyone to hear what I said. I hope the Liberal party has reformed since that time, because the day will come when those who took part in that booing, those who in those days were called "little Chicago", will bow their heads in shame. They just did not know; they just did not have sense enough to let themselves be told. There is no use talking any other way. If you are ever going to begin to remove the causes of war you must start at the causes of war.
On March 23, 1945, we were discussing the San Francisco conference in this house. I took part in that debate and I am reported on page 155 of Hansard of that day as saying:
I have mentioned three conditions under which Social Crediters favour an international organization. Fourth, each member undertakes to prohibit its nationals from owning or controlling any property or economic undertaking in another sovereign country.
Supply-*National Defence
That is a rather new way to approach this problem, is it not? Believe me, if we are going to approach this problem on a realistic basis we shall have to start right there. I went on further to say:
The significance of that measure for avoiding war will not be appreciated without a considerable amount of study and thought; but that is one of the most important measures, and if that stipulation is not embodied in the arrangements we make, all our attempts at attaining international peace will be futile.
Have my predictions been justified and warranted by what has occurred? Only too well; only too forcibly.
Fifth: Each nation undertakes not to export goods to any other nation, except in payment for imports from that nation, without the consent of that nation's government. That sounds as though it were going to touch somebody's pocket; consequently that stipulation will not be very acceptable. But the embodiment of the last two undertakings will go further towards producing a peaceful condition in this world than all the achievements of several San Francisco conferences.
Finally:	Each state undertakes to receive payment in goods and services for any debt owing to its nationals.
What a difference there would be in the world today if the United States would agree to that.
Do you need a Dumbarton Oaks, with an international police force, to enforce these regulations? All you need is good neighbourly sincere faith and honesty in approaching facts as they are in the world.
I said something more on that same page which I am going to quote if I have time. I am deeply concerned, along with all other members of the house, with removing the causes of war; but removing the causes of war does not have anything to do with building up a great international organization with a big police force to jam adverse policies down the throats of the nations and make them take it and like it. That is not finding a solution to their troubles.
I should like to turn to the document in question and consider it a little further. I shall refer to the section dealing with defence objectives of Canada, part III, and read from paragraph 18:
The attitude of the communists has simplified for all countries the problem of adjusting national interests to international needs.
If the communists have done that I wonder why we do not see more evidence of it in Canada. We can still pass rent regulations that paralyse people from coast to coast and make them wonder if there is anyone in Canada they can trust. If that is not preparing fruitful ground for communist seeds, tell me how you would do it any better, after

Supply-National Defence having made specific promises that such would not be done. In paragraph 19 I find these words:
The right way to preserve peace or to achieve victory is to work with others.
That is perfectly right. How skilful are these members of the government in telling us things which everybody knows are true, but how defective they are when it comes to proposing policies which will put into operation the general principles implied. I should like to turn now to part IV, page 15, paragraph 49, reading in part as follows:
Again in proportion to population the present strength of our navy reserve divisions, reserve army units and air force auxiliary squadrons are larger than the corresponding forces in Britain.
What does that mean? Here we are in Canada with the goods, resources human and material, to outdo, I imagine, ten to one what the British can do, and we are saying that we feel we have achieved something really big when our expenditure, in proportion to our population, is equal to Great Britain's. It is fantastic, is it not, when you look at it? It indicates a lack of a realistic approach to the whole matter.
I should like to turn now to part VI, page 25, paragraph 105, where, referring to the greatest bottleneck in meeting a future emergency, it says that:
... it would be in trained tradesmen. Steps are being taken to increase their numbers.
That is entirely laudable, but the minister has not told us how many trained tradesmen we have, whether or not the number we have is adequate for the needs of the times, and how many we have in reserve in case we are suddenly confronted with war. We shall have to be in operation producing munitions within two days after the next war commences. We shall not have fifteen or eighteen months to tinker around the way we did in the last war. I wonder if the minister can tell us exactly how many trained men he has, how many he has in training who would be ready, say, in three months, six months, one year, and so on, and why he thinks the number he has is adequate. This is the kind of thing I want to know. Some of my sons will be in the next war; I am concerned about the matter. My family will be in danger; I am concerned. I cannot just take nice smooth-sounding phrases and be lulled to sleep.
May I turn now to part VII, page 29, paragraph 127, which reads:
Contracts have been arranged with Canadair Limited for the purchase of 100 F86A's at a cost of $30,211,190, which does not include the cost of engines, armament and radios. The work has already begun on the construction of this aircraft.
Suppose Russia were to strike six weeks from today. How many of these aircraft
IMr. Blackmore.]

would be available? I really would like to know that. I realize that probably the minister might be divulging secrets which it would be inadvisable to divulge, but that is the kind of thing I want to know when I approach the whole problem of preparation for war. When we start to fight we shall need munitions right away. At page 31, paragraph 136, I find the following:
It has been decided to produce new high-powered radar equipment in Canada, thereby giving to Canadian electronic manufacturers experience and capacity invaluable in the event of an emergency.
When do they intend to begin to make this high-powered radar equipment? That is what I want to know. It has been decided; probably it was decided five years ago.
Paragraph 139 reads in part:
In 1948-49 we let contracts for 2,160 married quarters and in addition there were 273 housing units under construction at the end of the year.
That sounds all right, but I should like to know what was the average cost to the government of constructing each of these houses. I should like to know where they are located.
In paragraph 140 we are told:
Although we have added 70 per cent to reserve army accommodation during the last ten years, there is still a great shortage.
How great? We really would like to know that.
Paragraph 141 reads:
For a good many years to come, expenditures on construction will constitute a major item in the defence program.
Bless my soul, we all knew that! It seems to me I knew that when I was fourteen. Paragraph 141 continues:
We have to accommodate seven or eight times the numbers we had before the war,-
I should think we would all know that.
-and have much larger requirements for operational units, stores, hangars, training establishments-indeed every type of construction in every part of the country.
Why on earth did the minister waste our time telling us that?
In the closing paragraph on page 32 I find these words:
This network, furnished with modern radio teletype equipment extends throughout Canada and connects Canada with other countries.
Well and good; but I want to know if it extends adequately to meet our needs in case of an attack in any particular area of Canada. There are a good many other things I want to say, particularly as to paragraphs 148, 149, 150, 151 and 152, but I will probably direct my questions concerning them to the minister some time later.
In conclusion, I advise the minister to advise the cabinet, while yet there is time, to go about discovering means of satisfactorily

distributing the goods Canada is able to produce. Let them set to work to find out how to make what is physically possible actually financially possible in this country. As matters are going now we are approaching the time when our production will exceed our consumption, just as it did before the depression both in Canada and in the United States; then the more goods we have the poorer we shall be, just as we were at that time. Everyone must realize that this statement is sound.
What are we going to do about it? That is the question. Are we going to tinker along with the outmoded philosophies of finance that have filled the minds of the ministers up to the present time, or is it possible for them finally to grow some new wood? When they have learned how to distribute our surplus goods in Canada then let them tackle the problem of how to distribute Canada's surplus goods to the various nations which need them because they are starving, whether or not those needy nations are able to get our dollars with which to pay for them.
When they have finally discovered how to solve this problem let them send a delegation to the United States to talk to President Truman and other men there who are concerned with the same question. Let them inform those people what they have found, and they will make a genuine contribution toward the removal of the major cause of war, and will be putting themselves in line to reap the reward of that hope which General Bradley expressed as being a possibility in our time.
I shall say no more at the present time, Mr. Chairman, but shall probably have something else to say later on.
