speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the outset of my remarks I should like to quote two short sentences from the Mainguy report, as follows:
Although this report in the very nature of things is bound to be critical, it must not be assumed that there are not many reasons for great national pride in the achievements of the Canadian navy, past and present, and in the men who inherit and guard its traditions.
Then a little further on:
If, therefore, we have stressed what is wrong, it should not be forgotten that a great deal also is overwhelmingly right.
If we substitute for "report" the word "remarks" or "criticism", and for "Canadian navy" substitute "defence forces," these two sentences I think will apply to what I have to say, and I think to most of what may be said by members of the opposition. My conception of our job is that we should point out to the government what we think is wrong with our defence policy and our defence 45781-107
Supply-National Defence forces, and offer suggestions as to improvements which may be made. This makes it necessary that our remarks be critical.
In going about the country, in railroad compartments, people's homes and so on, when any general discussion of the question of defence comes up I have found that ordinarily three questions are asked. First, what is our defence policy? Second, what commitments have we for defence under the Atlantic pact? Third, have we the forces we need to meet those commitments? The people of this country as a whole do not know what our defence policy is. I am not too sure that I know what it is. Certainly I do not know the answers to the other two questions, nor do I think they are known to any members of this house, except the members of the government. It seems to me one of the first things the government should do is announce to this country what our responsibilities are under the Atlantic pact. Having definitely outlined those responsibilities, then let them say what defence forces we have to meet those responsibilities. If that were done I am sure it would be much easier to get the men required for our defence forces, both permanent and reserve, and I think the government also would have the full support of all the people of Canada in the expenditures it might be necessary to make in order to meet those commitments. As it is, the general public do not know the answers to those questions. As a result there is a great lack of enthusiasm on the part of the young men of this country toward military service.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock. PRIVATE BILLS
The house resumed, from Friday, November 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Maybank for the second reading of Bill No. 66, respecting Alberta Natural Gas Company.

To go on,
Mr. Speaker, with my third and concluding speech of the current series on this Bill No. 66, last week I mentioned the fact that the life of the Turner valley oil field had been cut down considerably by the lack of foresight with respect to the conservation of the gas, and the fact that the life of the field is now estimated at approximately ten years. The requirements of the cities of southern Alberta have been jeopardized to such an

Alberta Natural Gas Company extent that, in the very near future, they are going to be forced to pipe gas down from the newer oil fields in northern Alberta.
So much for the wastage of the gas itself. There is another and probably more important reason for the conservation of the natural gas. This gas is used for the bringing up of the oil to the surface; it is estimated that for every barrel of oil taken out of the older fields, nine remain in the ground because the pressure of the natural gas has been used up by the wastage. Contrary to common belief, the oil does not appear in pools or lakes under the surface; rather, it comes in a porous rock which looks much like honeycomb. When your well is drilled, the natural gas pressure which has been building up over a period of millions of years forces the oil up into the well. As the pressure diminishes, the pressure of the salt water forces it up in between the oil in the porous limestone of the well itself. As a result, you have nothing left except salt water in your well.
The gas pressure comes in two different ways. The first is in a pocket of gas above the oil-bearing rock. The second type is dissolved right in the oil as a result of pressure. When the well is drilled the pressure is relieved and the gas naturally forces the oil up into the well. In the case of a gas pocket, gas may be retrieved at the well head, forced back down by means of pressure pumps, and used again to create sufficient pressure for the bringing up of the oil.
A recent survey made by the Gulf Oil Company has placed the known reserves in Alberta at 2,000 billion cubic feet. That sounds like a large amount of gas, but actually when the needs of the oil industry are considered, it is not a great deal. What gas we have must be conserved until we are assured that we have sufficient for our own needs and for the proper oil production.
There are some members, Mr. Speaker, who possibly think that I have been attempting to talk this bill out, but that is not true. My main point in speaking on this bill is to show the need for proper conservation methods. As for the incorporation of this company or any other company like it, we have no objections. We are in favour of incorporating any number of these pipe line companies. We have full confidence in the Alberta government and in the Alberta conservation board, and in their ability to determine how much of the gas may be exported out of Alberta to other parts of Canada and, after the Canadian needs are assured, how much may be shipped outside Canada to consumers in the United States.

In rising to speak on this bill, Mr. Speaker, I wish to make it perfectly clear at the outset that I do so in what, to my mind, is the best interest of British Columbia. I know that one member from British Columbia expressed fear that Vancouver would not get the gas if this bill did not go through. Unlike that member I feel that, if this bill goes through in its present form, Vancouver will not get the gas inasmuch as it would be at the tail end of any proposed pipe line. I am therefore speaking more as to the route through which this pipe line is to go to the coast than as to the product to be carried through the pipe line.
I could possibly rightly and properly take up the question of who owns the gas and whether it should be banded over to private enterprise or whether it should be distributed by the government of the province of Alberta or the government of the province of British Columbia; but I am not going to do that. I feel that the interests of British Columbia are paramount, and to my mind they definitely come before the interests of the states of Oregon and Washington. I am convinced that our best interests are not served if this line goes, as is proposed, through Kingsgate and through the states that I have mentioned. The location of this line is as important today as was the location of the Canadian Pacific Railway eighty or ninety years ago. I understand the minister made the statement that he wants the gas to go to the best available market. But I am satisfied that if the people who plotted out the route for the Canadian Pacific Railway in those days had sought a market instead of service, they too would have gone through the states of Oregon and Washington because the facilities and the type of terrain were far better suited to a cheaper line to the coast than the one through the Rockies. But that thought was far from their minds. They wanted to develop their own country. I feel that this pipe line today must be used to develop our own country, and particularly the province of British Columbia. The future development of that province depends on this line. I am selfish enough to feel that the industries that will follow in its wake should be developed in our own country rather than in the United States. I am also satisfied that the company could possibly save a few million dollars, but I believe that the few million dollars they would save would not be more than 10 or 15 per cent of the total cost of the line; and this amount, taken over the period of years during which it will operate, will be a mere nothing. Any profits that may be lost in the immediate present will be more than

retrieved by the shorter line going through Canada compared with the one going through the states.
Then there is the question of maintenance and the cost of construction. These bring immediate valuable revenue to one country or the other. It will run into millions and millions of dollars. It will mean the pipes, the fittings, the labour in putting the pipes down, the labour in maintaining it and the labour in distributing it over a good many years. We can do with that labour in Canada, we can do with that outlet for labour, and we can do with the revenue that will be derived from the pipe line going through our own territory.
As I said, if the Canadian Pacific Railway had taken the same stand we would not have the flourishing valleys of the Kootenay, the Fraser and the Okanagan in the interior of British Columbia that we have today, and the country as a whole would have lost out. I am satisfied that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company in Trail, one of the biggest undertakings of its kind in the empire, would not have been established there, neither would it have flourished in British Columbia, if it had not been for the Canadian Pacific Railway giving it the necessary service.
Then we have the wealth that has been developed in the interior of British Columbia. That too can be directly attributed to the facilities offered by the railways in bringing in labour and machinery and taking out the raw material to be manufactured or processed as the case may be. The government of the day saw the possibility and their foresight has paid dividends ever since.
As I pointed out, I regard modern transportation as being streamlined by the use of the pipe line, and the route is just as important as the railway was. Along this route I can visualize many townships and developed municipalities bringing vast wealth to the interior of British Columbia, wealth that we know is possible through the actual presence there of fine lands, fine timber, fine mines and everything that goes to make a country prosperous. Surely that would be in the best interest of our own kith and kin in our own province.
A factory established in the Okanagan or in the Fraser valley would contribute far more to the welfare of this dominion, and particularly to British Columbia, than one established in Spokane or Wenatchee. That brings to my mind the saying that the city of Spokane was built on the wealth of British Columbia. That is practically true because that city was built on money invested to exploit our natural resources in the early days, both timber and mines. Today it is a
Alberta Natural Gas Company flourishing city. Similar cities may well be duplicated by this pipe line. That is one reason why I am going to fight to have this pipe line go through our own country. It is a modern Aladdin's lamp that conjures up new industry and contributes to prosperity.
I am not opposed to the sale of this product to our friends across the line. Neither will an all-Canadian route prevent their purchasing it, but it would mean that the line would enter the main consuming points in the United States from Vancouver instead of ending at Vancouver. I do not have to go into detail on that point because I think it is fairly obvious that the dead end of a line- it does not matter whether it is gas or oil or anything else-usually gets what is left after all the other customers have been satisfied. In this instance the last customer would be the cities of Vancouver, New Westminster and possibly some of the Fraser valley towns.
It is quite possible that the supply of this gas may peter out. I was pleased to hear my hon. friends tell us of the vast resources particularly of gas that are known to be in Alberta. If a shortage did arise and the service had to be cut, the cut would take place toward the end where the greatest cost of transferring the gas arises. The obvious place to cut would be on the last place to be served. Therefore Canadian consumers would be cut off from supply first. That would be the cities of British Columbia. I do not blame the company. They may or may not have to do it. I am assuming that if such a condition did come about British Columbia would suffer.
The Canadian consumers have a stake in this. I feel that Canada, when she develops her own natural resources, should have the first chance to use them. We can be generous because we cannot possibly use more than one-third of it, and we would give two-thirds to our neighbours. But let our neighbours take their turn, as we have for many years taken our turn on fuel oil, gas and anything else that we get from them. They too have been generous. We can be just as generous, but they looked after the United States first of all.
This bill would have my full support if it was changed to contain a clause that the line will traverse Canadian territory all the way to Vancouver and then cross over from Vancouver to Tacoma, Seattle and the towns that they have in mind. I say that because of the added revenue that will be derived from the line going through our own dominion. I mentioned some of the added revenue that would come along from the pipes themselves, namely, the valves and fittings that would be manufactured in this country. Then there
45781-107i

Alberta Natural Gas Company is the cost of maintenance which is an annual cost. But added to these is the potential increase in our actual income from definite industries that will be set up along this line.
So far as I am concerned it has not been made clear, if this pipe line goes through the state of Washington and the product re-enters British Columbia from a distributing point in Tacoma or Seattle or somewhere in between, whether the price to the Canadian consumer would be on the United States dollar basis, which would be to our detriment because we would have to meet that 10 per cent penalty; or whether it would be conveyed through in bond, as it were, to Vancouver and sold at the Canadian price. This point has never been made clear. But I would presume that logically the United States distributor at the point in Washington would redistribute to Vancouver, billing the Vancouver purchaser for the price of the gas plus the exchange value of the dollar. I believe it would be quite logical for them to do that because after all the United States businessman is in business for the profit there is in it. He is not going to sell at a loss to Canada if there is a difference of 10 per cent in the value of the money.
On the other hand, by delivering through Vancouver to the United States we would be charging the full cost of transportation from Alberta to Vancouver, and not only the full cost of transportation but all the other costs of handling at the distributing points. Then we would be distributing through a Canadian point rather than through a United States point.
Presumably there is a charge of so much per mile for conveying the gas, and that cost per mile would remain in Canada; otherwise it would be paid by Canadians to the United States part of the line.
In the Ottawa Citizen of November 2 an item appeared which was taken from the Medicine Hat News, which was obviously written by someone with a sound knowledge of the situation and a full appreciation of the potential value of our Alberta gas as an empire builder. Unfortunately this visionary empire is south of the border. I should like to quote from this item:
It may be that a deal will eventually be arranged between Alberta, Ontario and the federal authority for a reciprocal export-import arrangement whereby Alberta gas will be sold to Oregon and Washington on an exchange basis for Texas gas to Ontario. This would be a scheme on a national basis which would ensure that Canada as a whole would obtain benefit from Alberta natural gas deposits.
The same sort of exchange seems to be taking shape in the background of oil developments.
It suggests that Canada as a whole does not include British Columbia. Gas is going to the state of Washington, and in return the


province of Ontario is to receive gas from Texas. They talk of Canada as a whole. That is the point I wish to make.
Time and again we have sacrificed the west for the benefit of the eastern provinces. Maybe we are in the backwoods. Maybe we lose contact with what is taking place. But here is a definite plan, outlined by someone who thinks he knows what he is talking about, to use British Columbia, to sidestep us by taking gas to the coast, ignoring our need and making a deal whereby the province of Ontario would benefit. The article mentions that it would serve specific populous markets. These markets, it points out, do not exist in western Canada.
This may be quite true. It was true when the railway tracks were first laid. I understand that when those tracks were first laid across the prairies there were just a few buffalo, some sagebrush and very little else. But they had vision. I know they had no markets when they started out; and if the markets had not come and the country had not developed there would have been millions upon millions of dollars wasted in a futile effort in taking transportation to the west. But we know that you have to start somewhere.
The same argument applies here. While at the present time we have not the necessary markets in the west, there is no doubt in my mind that those markets would spring to life immediately if given a lifeline and the wherewithal to come to life. The railways led the way then, and I think the pipe lines can very well lead the way today. From the company's point of view, they would still have the west coast market. They would still be able to serve the very market they now seek to serve, from Tacoma to Seattle.
All we are seeking is an all-Canadian route to give that service. Then, the second part of the article I mentioned deals with the suggestion of a deal which, would give the final knock-out blow to our hopes in British Columbia. I cannot agree with the article when it refers to benefit to the whole of Canada. Neither can I be convinced that benefits to the states of Washington and Oregon are direct or indirect benefits to the Dominion of Canada.
Concentration of industry in the east has been a handicap in the development of the west. I am glad to hear and to see that certain firms are now opening up branches in the west, realizing that this handicap has been placed on our backs for too long. Not only that, I consider British Columbia has the greatest untapped reserve in this dominion; and we cannot tap that reserve and develop it until we have something like natural gas with which to do it. Climate, as we know,

is good out there all the year round. Our industries can function all the year round without handicap in winter and summer.
I come to another point. The companies claim that the cost per mile would be much greater-I understand around 15 per cent. But I should like to point out that traversing the route suggested, through Kingsgate, through the northern part of the state of Washington and to the distributing point outside Seattle would be 1,331 miles, while the all-Canadian route, following the railway, would be 940 miles, or roughly 400 less. That would take care of a good deal of the extra cost per mile in laying down the pipe line. I am not qualified to say what that extra cost would be. I understand the pipe is to be placed underground.
Then there are certain difficulties in connection with pipe lines. For instance, it is a favourite sport of hunters to take a pot shot at a pipe line almost anywhere, whether it be in the United States or in Canada, or Iraq. Hunters will always take pot shots at pipe lines, with the result that there is a tremendous upkeep cost, and patrolling .must be done. There would be fewer chances of such damage along the route in British Columbia than along the other route, and it is a shorter distance.
In conclusion let me make it perfectly clear, especially to those interested in the idea of having this pipe line, that I do not know the personnel, that I do not know where the capital is derived from, and that I am not very much interested in those points. All I am interested in is to fight for the province I represent-and I intend to do all I can in that way.
Here we are going to hand out a valuable asset, one which if properly handled can build up an empire. We are going to hand it, not to an enemy, true, but to a friendly competitive nation. But we have done this so often in the past-we are doing it with our pulp, with our concentrates and with our wealth in general-including our gold. The profits to be derived from the development of our raw materials and our natural products are thus turned over to a friendly nation, rather than retained in our own.
For this reason I am going to ask that this bill be held up until such time as the promoters of the scheme accept a provision whereby the line will go through dominion territory all the way to Vancouver. I should like to see this put to a vote. And if it is put to a vote, I should like to see it put to a democratic vote.
Oh, oh.

I mean a free vote is not a vote starting from the leaders of the parties, but
Alberta Natural Gas Company starting in the back row and going right around and finishing with the leaders of the parties, letting members vote as they wish. I am afraid most of us vote just as indicated.
If a free vote were given I am satisfied hon. members in this chamber would see the point I am trying to make, that we are either going to give away an asset to a friendly nation, or retain and develop one of the most prosperous, and potentially more prosperous, provinces in the whole of the Dominion of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to speak on this bill or any other pipe-line bill. I have no personal interest either in the five bills passed last spring or the two which have come before the house at this session. However, in view of events which have taken place in the house in connection with these bills, I do wish to express my personal opinion upon them,
I believe there has been an entire misconception of the purpose of the bill before us, and the others preceding it. If one were to incorporate a public company under a provincial or the dominion companies act, provided one were not asking for something unlawful, the charter would be automatically forthcoming. Then it would be up to the applicant to qualify his shares before the securities commission before he was allowed to sell them to the public. That is the normal procedure. There would be no reason to refuse a charter to anyone.
But in the case of a pipe line company under the Pipe Lines Act it is required that a company be incorporated by act of parliament. There is a direct reason why it should be incorporated by act of parliament, and it is that these companies are given very considerable power, particularly in the field oi eminent domain. That is, they have power of expropriation under the Pipe Lines Act. Accordingly it was considered desirable that companies of this kind should be incorporated before parliament so that in each case they could be examined if necessary, and a decision could be made in order that the act might be passed. Five of these acts were passed at the last session and, although I have not compared them word for word, I think they are all identical with this bill. They were all passed pursuant to the Pipe Lines Act and the wording in the separate acts followed the wording in the Pipe Lines Act. However, when those bills came up before the house no opposition was raised to the incorporation of those companies.
If this bill is passed by parliament it merely means that a legal entity is established. It seems that certain members of this house have decided that this company shall
1684	HOUSE OF
Alberta Natural Gas Company remain stillborn, shall never be given a chance to mature and grow up. I ask those hon. members to reconsider their attitude. Surely if five companies have been incorporated pursuant to the Pipe Lines Act any other people applying for a similar charter should be entitled to enter into this competitive field. It does strike me as being most unfair and discriminatory that at this stage we should say that this bill should not be passed and that the five legal entities already in the field should have a complete monopoly.
I stress again that I have no personal interest, legal or otherwise, in any of these companies, but I do think it would be establishing a bad precedent to refuse incorporation to this or any other company. There are many things that must happen once the legal entity is established. The company would have to go to the relevant board and cabinet of the province in question to obtain the necessary authorization. Similarly it would have to go before the board of transport commissioners to obtain approval to construct the pipe line.
It was intended that the Pipe Lines Act should guide the lives of these companies and that that authority should be vested in the board of transport commissioners, not in this parliament. I should like to read the relevant parts of section 11, which are as follows:
A company shall not, except as in this act otherwise provided, begin the construction of a section or part of a company pipe line, until,
(a)	the board has by order granted the company leave to construct the line;
(b)	the plan, profile and book of reference of the section or part of the proposed line have been approved by the board;
Obviously the board of transport commissioners has control over these companies, not parliament. It is quite clear that the purpose of the Pipe Lines Act was not to have parliament supervise every last detail of the incorporation of these companies, but to have parliament incorporate the companies and then leave the direction and control over the companies to the board of transport commissioners.
It would appear to me to be most unfair and discriminatory to attempt to talk out this bill at this stage. This is the normal procedure. The only difference between an incorporation under this bill and an incorporation under the Companies Act is that control over the company is given to the board of transport commissioners. I would not suggest for a single moment that hon. members of this house were interested in this or any other bill, but I do suggest that if they were interested parties to bills of this type their action would closely resemble the action we have witnessed in this house. I ask hon. members


to reconsider the fundamentals of this thing and decide whether in fairmindedness and fair behaviour they should not say: If this bill is in proper form, it should have our approval.
I did not interrupt the hon. member when he was speaking, but I should like him to name the five companies which were incorporated last year to transport oil and gas to the west coast.
Why not let him look it up.
You make your speech and I will make mine.

I would refer the hon. member to chapter 27 of the statutes of 1949, an act to incorporate the British American Pipe Line Company; to chapter 34, an act to incorporate Interprovincial Pipe Line Company; to chapter 36, an act to incorporate TransNorthern Pipe Line Company; to chapter 37, an act to incorporate Westcoast Transmission Company Limited; and to chapter 38, an act to incorporate Western Pipe Lines.
I hope I am not transgressing on the time that would be allotted to me to speak when I ask these questions.
No more questions can be allowed at this time. Is the house ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, I think there are some further observations which should be made before the question is put. As I understand it, the purpose of the bill before us is to incorporate a company whose objects do not appear clearly in the bill. When I say that I have in mind that the route proposed to be followed and the points from which the gas will be collected and delivered do not appear in the bill we are discussing. In this connection I should like to support what was said a few days ago by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), that before the house is called upon to approve or disapprove of the principle of this bill permitting the transportation of natural gas which originates in Canada we should know clearly where the gas is to be sold and the route by which it is to be transported.
I make these observations because I believe in the principle which has been stated by many hon. members in the past, that the natural resources of Canada should be made available to and preserved primarily for the people of Canada. It is on that principle that I base the remarks I intend to make tonight in connection with this bill.
Although it is not immediately apparent from the terms of the bill, we understand that this company will gather the gas in southern Alberta and take it by pipe line

through the United States to be distributed to cities there; then if anything were left it would be taken to the Pacific coast city of Vancouver. Not only will the route by-pass the interior of British Columbia; the users in Vancouver and other cities in the province will have available only what gas is left over after the needs of the points in the United States have been fully supplied.
The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones), who preceded me in this debate, made what I think were pertinent references to the history of the development of the western part of Canada. One of the features which stand out in that history is that if the founders of Canada, the pioneers of the nation, had not had faith in its future, which faith was not justified by the previous development of the country but was founded upon their determination and belief that they could and should build a great nation north of the 49th parallel, this country would not have existed today as a separate entity. I think we would be somewhat untrue to the faith and determination of those who went before us, and who built the nation, if we did not hold true to the principles they laid down in the days when the tasks and difficulties of constructing the country were so much greater than those which we face today.
In taking the position that Canadian resources must be reserved primarily for the development of Canada, one is not necessarily adopting a selfish or unreasonable attitude, and it should not be regarded as a slight to the United States of America. In fact it is nothing more than taking a lesson from the history of the development of Canada. We know quite well that the Canadian Pacific Railway, to come down to cases, would not have been built if it had not been that the fathers of confederation, those who insisted that Canada should exist as a separate nation, said that the lines of communication in the northern half of this continent should run east and west rather than north and south. They took that stand in spite of most serious obstacles, and carried it out in building a railway through the barrier of the Rocky mountains on to the Pacific coast.
As a result of their vision this country came into being, and the dream of confederation was eventually completed by the addition of the Pacific coast province as a part of Canada. It is not necessary for us to go back into history to remind hon. members of the fact that at one time it was somewhat questionable whether that Pacific coast province, or the southern portion of it at any rate, should belong to Canada or by virtue of geography to the nation south of the 49th parallel. In the same way that the country was built up and came into
Alberta Natural Gas Company being because of the determination to build a nation from Atlantic to Pacific, I think that we should insist upon developing that nation from the Atlantic to the Pacific and serving our people before we allow our resources to be diverted south of the border.
The hon. member for Yale has mentioned the potentialities of the province of British Columbia, climate, resources and people, affording a great natural market for industrial development. Such development has not taken place at the rate which we would desire to see, because of a combination of two factors. It is rather like the old question of which came first, the chicken or the egg. Must you have the population first in order to attract heavy industry, and after heavy industry power and other factors which will create an industrial economy, or must you have power and communications first in order to build up a population which will support the heavy industries that people have the vision to establish there? In my view, Mr. Speaker, the history of Canada shows that it is communications, power, transportation, which invariably come first in this country.
That has been the history of the development of the west. It was the history which followed upon the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It was the history which followed upon the building of the Canadian Northern, the Canadian Northern Pacific, and the Grand Trunk Pacific railways. While it is certainly true to say, particularly of the last three railway systems, that they fell upon hard times and for many years did not pay, and that it was necessary eventually for the dominion government to take them over and amalgamate them into the one Canadian National system, is there anyone in the house who will say that the country was badly served by the vision, inspiration and determination of the men who built those railway lines in advance of the actual population requirements? I am quite certain that no one will say the country was badly served, although it is perfectly true that these railways did go through a most difficult period before they were amalgamated and made into a paying proposition.
Anyone who is familiar with the history of the western area of Canada knows full well the part the railways played in the development of the country, and that at the present time they are paying lines because population, industry, agriculture and the economy generally have been built up to a point where they support and make it possible for the railways to be a revenue producing proposition in the same areas where at first they were bankrupt.
We from the west coast province believe that it is capable of much greater development in the future than has taken place in
1686	HOUSE OF
Alberta Natural Gas Company the past. We know the resources of the area; we know its potentialities; we know the great untapped areas which have not yet been subject to any development at all. Because we have contributed in the past to the development of the rest of Canada, because we have paid our willing tribute as a part of Canada to the predominantly industrial sections of the central part of the country, Ontario and Quebec, we feel it is not unfair for us to request that these portions of Canada, which have benefited by the advantages we were able to contribute to the development of confederation, should bear their share in developing the undeveloped parts of our province.
Although, on the basis of strict economics, it may be somewhat less profitable to insist that these pipe lines should be constructed through Canadian territory, and should serve Canadian markets, I leave the thought with the house that the development of a nation, if one has a patriotic idea of that development, never proceeds upon a basis of straight economics. If we had proceeded upon such a basis in the past Canada would not be an independent nation today. We believe Canada can become a much greater, more powerful and more independent nation than she is today, standing on her own feet, if she follows her own course of development. Because we believe in that and because we insist upon that, as far as we in the west are concerned, at any rate-and in this respect I certainly believe I can speak for my constituency-we feel that these pipe lines should serve Canadian markets and Canadian consumers before our resources are made available to those south of the border. Not being satisfied upon that point, I must oppose this bill.

Mr. Speaker, the constituency of Nanaimo may not appear to be directly affected by this bill, because it is on Vancouver island and I do not know whether it would be possible or practicable to pipe this natural gas under the strait of Juan de Fuca to that island. However,
I do know that the prosperity of Vancouver island depends very largely upon the prosperity of the city of Vancouver and the great hinterland of British Columbia. We are largely dependent upon the tourist trade, and that is not composed entirely of foreigners coming to our island. We are delighted to welcome people from other parts of British Columbia and other parts of Canada who come to enjoy our scenery and take advantage of our facilities for such sports as fishing, mountaineering and so on. Many people from the great cities of Vancouver and New Westminster spend their week ends and their 

holidays on Vancouver island, and particularly in my constituency. Their ability to come over to our island and enjoy the advantages we are able to offer depends entirely upon the prosperity of those two cities; and anything that will enhance that prosperity naturally reacts to the advantage of the people of Vancouver island.
So it seems to me that if in these somewhat difficult times we can make available to the people of the metropolitan area of Vancouver our natural resources, which can be transported there direct from another province, it will not only help the interior of British Columbia but will also benefit the pleasure resorts of Vancouver island. From the little I know about natural gas, I believe that when it is piped it can be tapped anywhere along the line and much of the gas can be diverted before it reaches its ultimate destination. Therefore I feel that we should route this pipe line direct from Alberta to the great cities of the Canadian Pacific coast instead of sending it through the friendly northwestern United States and allowing the huge cities of the states of Washington and Oregon to have first chance at this Canadian product which many of us believe should be developed for the benefit of Canadians rather than the benefit of those of another country, no matter how friendly that country may be.
I have travelled by motorcar, by train, by aeroplane and on foot over a great deal of the territory lying along the boundary between Canada and the United States, and I do not believe there are any insurmountable obstacles to a pipe line following the all-Canadian route. As has been pointed out already by previous speakers, that route is shorter than the United States route. It is not as well known or as well travelled, but that is largely because the roads are not so good.
Order. The hour for private and public bills having expired, the house will revert to the business under consideration at six o'clock.

subtopic: TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE WITH PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE WITH PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
If I might have leave to revert to motions, Mr. Speaker, in conformity with an undertaking I gave the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) at page 1318 of Hansard to table correspondence with the provincial governments in respect to housing, I now table that correspondence with all provinces, going back to the Prime Minister's letter to all provincial premiers dated March 2, 1949.


The house in committee of supply, Mr. Dion in the chair.
239. Grants to military associations, institutes and others, as detailed in the estimates, $227,150.

Before the house rose at six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I had been saying something about the three questions I found being brought up most frequently by the general public as far as defence matters are concerned; that is to say, what is our defence policy, what are our defence commitments under the Atlantic pact, and have we the forces to meet those commitments. Now I should like to go on and say something in reference to our defence policy.
I suppose the seven points the minister gave us this afternoon summarize our defence policy and give it as clearly as it has yet been placed before this house or the public. I presume those seven points are included in the white paper the minister tabled today. I am sorry I have not yet had an opportunity to see that document, and I shall certainly be most interested in reading it. However, I jotted down those points as the minister gave them. The first five were what might be called more or less general; that is, that the only possible aggressor is Russia; that any war would be a world war; that the best way to prevent war is to have strong forces; that in order to have strong forces with which to prevent anything in the nature of Russian aggression we must have the co-operative strength of the western world; and that Canada welcomes the Atlantic pact as giving that co-operative strength definite form. Then the sixth and seventh points might be said to be those under which the practical details of our defence policy would fall. We have had statements in this connection at various times. Roughly it comes down to this; that what Canada requires is a small but highly trained and efficient navy, air force and army, the navy capable of doing convoy, antisubmarine and anti-mine work, and the air force and army capable of meeting any diversionary raid. In other words, as the Ottawa Journal has in its headlines, "Sneak Red Attack Canada's No. 1 Defence Worry." That headline pretty well sums up the situation. The question whether the army and the air force are in a situation to meet a sneak attack of that sort is one which I shall come to a little later on.
In addition to these permanent forces which I have been dealing with up to this time, however, there is also the question of the reserve forces. As to the navy and the air force, the reserve forces are comparatively small and, as far as I know, the
Supply-National Defence plans do not envisage large reserve forces for those two arms of the service. But the plans do envisage fairly large reserve forces for the army, running to a strength of five or six divisions, and in the event of emergency capable of rapid expansion into a strong hitting force which could be used for fighting wherever the theatre of war happens to be-and which everybody hopes will be, as the minister said this afternoon, as far away from Canada as possible.
During past sessions, and particularly since the post-war defence force was brought into being, we have directed various questions to the government with the general object really of finding out to what extent this force, about which the minister was always talking and to which a great deal of publicity was given, was in being; in other words, whether we had a navy which could do its job and whether we had an army and air force which could do the job, or whether we had not. The general impression given was that we had those forces, that we were all right and that in the event of one of these sneak attacks it could be repelled, and so forth.
In speaking on defence in the budget debate, the minister said that he had answered all questions which had ever been asked in connection with these matters, except one which I happened to ask and about which there was some question last year. I do not want to get into any argument about the number of questions that were not answered. I can assure the minister that I could turn up a few others that were not answered. I must say that, as to questions which were asked by me and which were not answered orally here in the house or in writing in reply to the written questions on the order paper, the minister or his parliamentary assistant of that time would frequently come to see me or telephone me and say: We will not give this information in the house, we will not put it in the form of a written answer, but we will give it to you privately. I wanted to say that, in order to be completely fair in this matter. That happened frequently; but there, were some cases in which it did not happen. In spite of what the minister has said to the effect that he had answered all questions, the fact remains that the answers given orally in this house, the written answers given, and the information given to a person privately when he wants to ask a question about some particular thing, such as the number of tanks we had or something else, are not sufficient to give any member of the house, and particularly the house as a whole, any complete, good, balanced picture of what the situation is with regard to our defence forces.

Supply-National Defence
In this general committee of the house it is impossible to get sufficiently detailed information. For one thing, ordinarily we cannot take enough time to get it. Only today we were informed that it is hoped that the session will be over by December 3. We have some thirty or forty bills still on the order paper, and we have practically all the estimates yet to be dealt with. In this general committee it is impossible to get the detailed information which is necessary to give any member of this chamber the knowledge that he should have in order to be able to consider intelligently the situation with regard to our defence forces. This inability of members to get information is, I think, to a large extent the result of the set-up, the way our business is done here, and so forth. That is one reason why the members of this party for some three years now have been pressing for a defence committee of this house to be set up, in which we could see the heads of the services, could get the detailed information that many of us would like to have, and could find out what our situation is.
To leave that point, Mr. Chairman, the contention of several of us on this side of the house in the past has been that we did not have the defence forces which the general public and in fact the house had been led to expect that we possessed; and our contention is that in fact we still have not those forces.
As to the navy, in spite of the Mainguy report I think it is probably an exception from that point of view. As far as I know, I think the navy is a fighting force in being. In other words, it could go out tomorrow and fight. If it were given a week, ten days or a month, it could probably fight fairly efficiently. There might be some ships which were not in good shape; nevertheless so far as I know, it is a fighting force in being. In spite of certain deficiencies which have been shown up in this report, in the navy I think we probably have something like what we have paid for and what we should have.
When we come to the army and the air force, I do not think that situation has prevailed during the past three years, and I do not think it prevails at the present time. As far as I know, the fighting units in the army and air force are lacking in trained personnel, and are particularly lacking in equipment. They could not go out and fight tomorrow; they could not go out and fight in a week's time; and unless the equipment were forthcoming in fairly short order from the United States or some place else, they would not be able to go out and fight in several months' time.
[Mr. Harkness.i
In my opinion, that is not good enough. Under the defence policy as enunciated by the minister, we were supposed to have an army and an air force capable of meeting any diversionary raid on this country. Last session and the session before we were assured that we had a force designed to do that, and that we had an airborne brigade group. As a matter of actual fact, as I say, I do not think we have that. I think the members of the house should be able to get the information required in order to know whether we have a force or whether we have not, and to know just what is the situation.
I should like to say one or two things further in connection with this matter. From the casual information that I have been able to pick up-I have not sought it out or looked for it; it has just come to me because I know a large number of people who have served and are serving in the defence forces -I think considerable progress has been made in the last six or eight months with regard to the army. As far as I know, the number of men has increased considerably, and as a result their training has been considerably improved. I know that about a year ago most of the permanent force units of any size in this country were at half strength or less, as the result of which it was impossible for them to train efficiently; and of course it would have been hopeless for them to attempt to fight. I know also that at the present time at least some of those units are up to full strength; and from what I have been able to see of them, I think their training is fairly good. That is encouraging. As I say, that is just information that, as far as I am concerned, I have gained casually and so on. But on the basis of that I think a considerable amount of progress has been made in the army during the last eight months or so. I am glad of that, but so far as the situation in the air force is concerned I do not know whether there has been a similar improvement or not. One thing I do know is that their equipment situation is still not good.
I should now like to say something about the numbers of officers and other ranks who are employed in headquarters of various sorts. Last year a return was made to a question of mine which is now out of date, therefore I will not bother quoting it. But the number of officers and other ranks in the three services who were employed at National Defence headquarters or at command headquarters or at naval division headquarters was considerable. It was a big proportion of the total number of personnel in all three services. I was glad to see that the Mainguy report took some

cognizance of that and made a recommendation in connection with it which appears on page 61 under "administration." It reads as follows:
The needs of the modern navy, in general, and the mass of administrative detail, paper work and committee work involved, have placed upon valuable naval officers an undue burden of administrative detail. In Britain the navy commands the services of a number of high-ranking and competent civil servants. Although difficulty may be encountered in creating civilian positions of high enough level and salary to attract the most desirable entrants, we feel that there would be a considerable improvement in efficiency and a substantial saving both in money and in valuable manpower if the British system were followed.
Great benefits would flow to all three services through releasing from office desks here in Ottawa, and at command headquarters and at various other headquarters across the country, a large number of officers and other ranks who are held there at the present time doing administrative detail work. I trust that that is a move which will be made and made just as rapidly as possible.
I have talked to several people in the services about what I would call the top-heavy organization of the defence forces. We have far more people in headquarters, and in things of that sort, than we have in the actual fighting units. Most of them have said, "Yes, it is too bad that is the situation, but unfortunately we must have a headquarters set-up which, if a war broke out, could be rapidly converted to handle a large army of five or six divisions." How are we going to get away from this kind of thing? Since we have to cut our coat according to our cloth-our resources-I think that in the meantime it would be much better to use the manpower available, and the manpower which we can afford to pay for, mainly in actual fighting units rather than having this large administrative and command set-up which will really come into operation and be used only if we raise a large army.
I should now like to deal with the reserve force. To begin with, I should like to pay a tribute to the officers and other ranks who devote a considerable portion of their time to working in reserve units throughout the country. At very considerable sacrifice to themselves in most cases they are doing an extremely valuable work which all too often the general public in their own communities do not appreciate and do not thank them for. Without the counterparts of these men in 1939 I think everyone admits that we could not have mobilized the first and second divisions with the rapidity with which we did, and the subsequent divisions afterwards. They are the people upon whom any large mushrooming of the defence forces,
Supply-National Defence particularly of the army, must be built, and they deserve all the encouragement that can be given them. One of the great difficulties, in fact the greatest difficulty so far as the reserve units are concerned

and it is of the army particularly that I am speaking-is the difficulty of getting men.
When the minister spoke this afternoon he said that the recruiting was satisfactory; that they had been getting all the men they wanted except in the reserve forces. I doubt whether they have been getting all the men they wanted in the last three years, otherwise we would have had the permanent defence force filled up far sooner. We have been trying for about three years now to get it filled up and it is still not filled up. However, I think everybody admits that there has been extreme difficulty in getting men into the reserve units. The recruiting campaigns which have been put on have been flops.
In Calgary we have had two or three army weeks that I remember, during which the various units came down town with pieces of their equipment. This equipment was put in prominent places such as busy street corners and so forth to be seen by the people. Posters were put up. Advertisements were put in the newspapers. Talks were given on the radio, and so on, all designed to draw in recruits for both the reserve forces and the permanent forces. So far as the reserve forces are concerned, these means were just hopeless. Very few recruits were secured as a result of them, in Calgary at any rate. I understand the same thing was true across most of the country.
One of the things I object to is that when questioned on this matter the minister has always said, and this has been going on for the last two or three years: "Our policy is to train officers and n.c.o.'s. We do not care about getting a lot of men in. What we want to do is to train a good solid corps of officers and n.c.o.'s; after that we shall go out and get the men; but that is what we have to do first." That has been a very convenient excuse, a very convenient story, but actually that is all it is. You cannot train officers and n.c.o.'s unless you have some men for them to work with.
It is just a hopeless business having a full strength of officers and n.c.o.'s in reserve force units and have them come down to the armouries once a week and find five or ten men to work with. They get discouraged. There is nothing for them to do in the way of training except to talk to one another. They get discouraged, and in many cases they quit or they come only infrequently. In order for an officer or an n.c.o. to get training he must have some men to work with. That has

Supply-National Defence been one of the difficulties with the reserve units. They have not had the men. This story that they do not want the men until they get these people trained is just so much eyewash. Actually a very large proportion of the officers and n.c.o.'s in our reserve force units are men who had years of service overseas during the war. In other words, they were trained men. It is true that the number of new officers taken in in the last year has been increasing, but some of the n.c.o.'s, actually the bulk of them, are men who had a good deal of actual training right on the battlefield. What they needed to keep the units going, to keep them interested, was some men to work with, and they have not had them. There must be some reason for this.
The recruiting campaigns put on have been unsuccessful. I think the basic reason is this. The young men of this country have not been joining the reserve force units in any numbers because they have no real belief that they are needed in these units. They have not been convinced that it is their duty to serve this country in a reserve force unit. I think a considerable number of them are convinced of that fact. They were convinced during the war when they enlisted in large numbers.
I believe we are going to have great difficulty in getting any reasonable number of men in our reserve forces. I have one suggestion as to how in my view this could be corrected to some extent. The Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence might make very definite appeals to the young men of this country to joint the reserve force units, and then follow that up by enlisting the help of service clubs, newspaper editorialists, schools and the like. If this were done we would have much better response than we have had thus far.
The main thing is that these young men have to be convinced that they are wanted, that there is a duty for them to perform; and when they are convinced of that they will come forward to do it. That is one possible way of having the message put over. Certainly to date this has not been done.
I should like to say something next about certain defence deficiencies which were shown up by Exercise Eagle. The minister had something to say about this when he spoke a few days ago on matters of defence, as reported at page 1413 of Hansard. I shall not read all he said, but the point he made was that this exercise was designed to test stability and the state of training of officers and men of the P.P.C.L.I., the scale and state of training of the officers and men of the air force, and the work of the staffs which planned and carried out the exercise. He indicated that from that

point of view it was a great success. I have no fault to find with that statement. From those points of view it was successful.
However, the minister goes on to say that it was those three things the exercise was designed to test-
-and the reports by my officers indicate that in these respects the exercise was very successful indeed.
What the minister does not say-and should have said, I think-is that whether the exercise was intended as a test of the fact or not, in actual fact it showed that we have not a properly equipped force to deal with a diversionary raid. In other words, it shows that we have not the very things that, as indicated by these newspaper headlines tonight, the minister himself says in his white paper we need-an integrated air force, and army airborne troops, properly equipped to meet a diversionary raid.
It was not intended that this exercise should show we did not have that; I have no doubt about that. Nevertheless it did show it, I suggest, and it is up to the minister's department to make good that deficiency, and to make it good very rapidly.
It also showed up another thing, namely equipment shortages. I am not going to go into the various details concerning aircraft, and so on. However, those equipment shortages were definitely thrown in the public eye. As a result they have disquieted the general public-and that is easily understood.
One of the reasons the country generally was disturbed over the report was as the result of the general impression which has been left during the past two years to the effect that we had an efficient force which could do this very job the exercise showed the force used could not do. Certainly we did not have any better force to use in place of the one used. We had no better infantry battalion and no battalion better trained than the P.P.C.L.I. for airborne operations.
In this connection I would say one further word about a matter mentioned in the Mainguy report, namely shortages of kit. At page 54 a paragraph deals with shortages of kit for those newly entering the navy. I do not know why there should have been such shortages. We had large quantities of naval clothing and the like during the war. There must have been a great deal of that on hand. And if we did not have it, surely there has been plenty of time in the period since, if stores were exhausted, to get new ones.
I find it difficult to understand why it was impossible to equip these people, or to re-equip them when their stuff was worn out-kit, clothing and so on. This should

not have happened. What is the state of affairs in this connection so far as the air force and the army are concerned? Are they similarly short of kit? If so, why? Certainly if an emergency of any sort were to develop and there were a shortage of kit for permanent force personnel, it is easy to envisage the bad situation we would have.
I remember that when we were mobilized in 1939 the men of my unit went around without uniforms for a considerable length of time. There were no uniforms for them at all; and this condition was not corrected until the first issue of battledress came along in November, I believe it was, 1939. There should not be any repetition of that; there is no need for it, particularly with the large amounts spent for defence purposes at the present time.
I would also mention the provision of armouries. A considerable number of reserve force units have been badly handicapped in their training and recruiting because of lack of armouries. I know the construction of armouries has become difficult because housing and barracks accommodation have had prior claims. However, I would ask the minister to meet this need for armouries accommodation as rapidly as this can be done. Particularly would I recommend the provision of small or makeshift armouries in small places where there is considerable interest in reserve force units and where they have been carrying on under extreme difficulty. I believe it would be possible to give a considerable number of these places armoury accommodation without any great expenditure of either funds or materials. In many cases all that has been asked by these people is that huts on abandoned air force stations, and the like, should be moved over, rebuilt and adapted to their purposes.
I should like to make reference to some remarks of the minister concerning unification. At page 1415 of Hansard he took a good deal of credit to himself for the speed of unification, and stated:
With regard to organization, I believe I can say without fear of successful contradiction that in the work of unification, co-ordination and the streamlining of our forces, navy, army and air forces, the Department of National Defence of Canada has made more progress than any other country in the world.
I do not doubt the truth of that statement. However, I suggest it is not a matter for great congratulation on the part of the minister. I do not know why we should not have made more progress than any country in the world: we had far less to unify, it is quite clear that the less by way of forces we have to unify, the more rapid progress we can make in that regard. If we have

National Defence only one ship and one squadron of aircraft and one army battalion we can unify them in short order. The reason we have been able to make more rapid progress lies in the fact that we have had so little to unify.
In the same speech the minister dealt with a request made by the leader of this party, and many other members of it, for a defence committee of the house. As reported on page 1414 of Hansard the minister said:
I would welcome a committee on defence or anything else, but I do not believe that is the proper method of conducting business in parliament or of running the defence forces of this country.
I should like to make it clear that in asking for a committee there was no thought that the committee would be running the defence forces of this country. No one ever had that in mind. The purpose of the committee would be to get information to enable hon. members of the house to see the full picture of the defence situation. Any idea that the minister or his officials may have that it is being suggested that the committee would take over the running of the defence forces is completely wrong.
Before I close I should like to say something about civilian defence, a matter about which I spoke at considerable length a year ago and more briefly during the throne speech debate. It is a matter on which this house has never had any information so far and I should like to ask the minister to make as full a statement as possible on what has been done and what is being done in this connection. I know that General Worthington was appointed civilian defence co-ordinator and has been travelling about the country as well as going to the United States and Europe to study civilian defence methods that are being followed. I know General Worthington, and I am sure he is doing a good job, but I should like to know how much support he has had and what else besides appointing him is being done in connection with this important matter.
I think the government has failed to realize that the people of the country are concerned over this. This is not merely a question for debate here among a few people who are interested in defence; it is something which affects everybody in this country, it is something in which a large number of people are interested. The possibility of an atomic bomb attack in another war has been more or less in the thoughts of a large number of people and most of them are wondering what measures, if any, are being taken for their protection and the protection of their families in the event of such a catastrophe.
This is something which should have the fullest publicity. Definite measures should be taken for the evacuation of people and for the stockpiling of tents and other materials

Supply-National Defence which could be used in an emergency, of medical supplies, of foodstuffs and so on. My own view is that it is more important to carry out these civilian defence measures than it is to develop our defence forces. They should have first priority because the basic strength of this country is in the civilian population. As an indication of what people are thinking in connection with this matter I should like to read a letter which I received the other day, under date of November 3, as follows:
I am sending you a cutting from the Calgary Herald which outlines my own view as to what could happen if the communists wanted to start a sudden coup in this country before war was declared, and it is to be hoped that matters similar to this are being taken care of by the defence authorities in charge.
You can imagine what would happen in our fair city if the Calgary power dam, the Glenmore dam and other similar projects which supply our water were blown up. It would be too late to think about these things after and steps should be put into effect at all times to watch for and control such projects "while there is time."
To my knowledge, I have never seen the writer of that letter. The clipping which was enclosed dealt with the action taken at Denver, Colorado, by the national guard there to build up civilian cells, as it were, to counteract communist cells and to prevent any sabotage. That idea, I think, is well worth looking into. It certainly indicates a real interest by the people in civilian defence.
In this morning's Globe and Mail there is a report which reads as follows:
Fire Dangers Dim A-Bombs, says Worthington
The dangers of fire far overshadow those of atomic radiation in any potential enemy raid on a Canadian city, Major General F. F. Worthington told the engineering institute of Canada today.
The people right across Canada should be given information as to the best way of fighting fires which might develop as the result of an atomic bomb attack. I was glad to see that apparently the people of Toronto have taken this matter into their own hands to some extent and have formed a committee which is investigating this matter of civilian defence. Apparently they are making some progress in getting information out to the general population in Toronto and advising as to ways and means in which they can help themselves. I am wondering how much help these people have had from the Department of National Defence and how much interest is being shown by the department in having similar committees appointed in Canadian cities, particularly in the larger centres.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened to the various speakers this afternoon and evening and one thing has struck me. Each of the opposition speakers has picked out a portion of the picture with
[Mr. Harkness.l

which to deal. There was probably a certain amount of truth in what he had to say, but if the story of Nelson putting the telescope to his blind eye has any significance or symbolism, it is that he refused to be stampeded by what he saw of a portion of the picture. In his mind's eye he looked for the whole picture and went on to victory.
Naturally, for security reasons, the defence estimates cannot be discussed in the same way that the agriculture estimates could be; but hon. members have a responsibility to their constituents and there are many ways in which they can see the whole picture and thus carry out their responsibilities. We all read the newspapers and can see what goes on in other countries. We are able to make our own decisions as to whether this job is being well handled. I cannot understand anyone blocking unification, and we have all seen what has happened since the last war. One great lesson that was learned was the necessity for co-operation between the various services. That co-operation has continued and in this country it has reached a peak not equalled by any other country in the world.
We saw what happened in the naval inquiry and we know that something really came out of that. This afternoon the minister mentioned the conversion of Royal Roads and the reopening last year of R.M.C. as the Canadian services colleges. When the R.M.C. closed in 1942 the last number on the rolls was 2,828, and over 2,000 of those ex-cadets served their country on active service in all quarters of the world.
I feel that is one of the reasons why the minister made it a part of his policy to reopen the college. Six weeks ago I had the opportunity of visiting it on the occasion of the governor general unveiling a plaque in memory of those ex-cadets who are a part of those whom we commemorate today. At that time I had a chance to see just what had been done in the short space of a year, and I was most pleased with what I saw. At the annual dinner of the ex-cadet club the minister made a toast to the college, and it is from a person's words that you can see how he thinks. The words he spoke that night revealed to me why Canada's defence thinking is in the front rank of the world today, not excepting any country. At this time I want to commend the government for its defence program, and I also want to commend the minister for reopening that college. I want to read to you a portion of what he said. These are the words of the present Minister of National Defence:
In conclusion there is one thing I would like to emphasize. In the years between the wars there was often a dividing line, a cleavage, between members of the permanent and reserve forces. There

was also frequently a cleavage between graduates of R.M.C. and those who had not had that good fortune, as you would regard it. Then there was a division between the navy, the army and the air force. Finally there was the division between the services and civilians. All those divisions I want to see wiped out. At the services colleges I want to see the three services working as one team. Perhaps they might keep the habit. In summer training I want to see men from Royal Roads and R.M.C. mixed up with men from the universities and from the reserve units, in the ships, at the camps, and on the flying fields, doing the same work, learning to like each other because they know each other.
I want to see active and reserve forces working side by side, wearing the same clothes, getting the same pay, achieving the same standards ... as citizens and service men. And because we shall have done these things, then we shall see no difference between members of the civilian and the service community-both are citizens-but the services will earn the respect and support they deserve because in addition to being citizens they serve their country all the time.
Fellow members, these are the words of the minister who is responsible to us for the program of Canadian defence. I have read between the lines as to what is taking place, and I am satisfied that the program is in good hands.

There are a couple of points I want to raise. I think it is generally agreed in all parts of the house that we should have preparedness. The division of opinion seems to be as to just what constitutes preparedness having regard to another war. To my mind there are two points which I think are most important. The first one is the co-operation and co-ordination of our forces with the forces of other countries which think as we do. The minister has stated that if we have another war it will be a world war. In a world war the contribution of a country the size of Canada, even though we think we are pretty important, is small compared with the total contribution. Unless we have co-ordination between our forces and the forces of those who may be our allies, I do not think we can contribute as much as we could if such co-operation took place in time. Even though we have to sacrifice some of our national pride, it seems to me that, in the world as it is constituted today, any enemy we may have to face is going to be one who will drive from one central point with one central objective, and with complete co-ordination of their forces. Unless we can meet that by co-ordination and co-operation, we shall do just as we did in the last two wars. We shall sacrifice thousands of lives in getting to the point where we can meet a concentrated attack.
The other point I want to mention is that the next war, if there is one, will be won or lost on the technical advances made in the next few years, not on our skill in the use of the weapons with which we won the last war.
Supply-National Defence Too often our objective between wars has seemed to be the training of people to use the weapons with which we won the previous war. No war is ever won by the use of the weapons with which the previous war was won. That is the lesson which we should have learned from history, and it seems to me that in spending money on our defence we should do so intelligently.
For instance, the distribution of our defence dollar, it seems to me, is something about which we should certainly make inquiries.
In 1948-49, 6 per cent of our defence dollar was spent for defence research, and in 1949-50, 5 per cent of our defence dollar is to be spent for that purpose. To me that is nonsense. If it is true, and it is, that wars are won by technical knowledge and development, then that is too small a proportion of our defence dollar to spend on the research which will be necessary to win the next war. 1 would say that three or four times that proportion would be well spent in technical research.
We know that probably our greatest single drawback in the first and second world wars was the fact that we lacked the necessary new equipment. We had plenty of Ross rifles and rifles of other makes in the first world war, but we lacked artillery. It was only when Lloyd George organized the economy of England, and reorganized the production of that country, thereby developing the artillery and shells that were necessary to win that war, that we were able to make advances. The same is true of the last war. It was two or three years before we developed the production of the materials necessary to win the war. Surely we will not allow ourselves to get into the same position in the event of another war. Surely we should have learned our lesson from the last two wars. Surely we should have learned that technical research and the development of a strong economy, in which we are producing the essential materials to win a war, is the best preparedness that we can have in Canada.

It seems to me that there has been general agreement, as one would expect, with regard to the objectives of Canada's defence forces, and the necessity of spending large amounts of money in order that such forces may be adequate. I am sure that no one, least of all the minister and his supporters on the government side, wishes to spend money to no good purpose. Certainly members of the opposition regard it as their duty to see that every dollar spent is spent wisely and to good purpose. We are all agreed that heavy expenditures on defence requirements are necessary, and we are all prepared to support such expenditures if we are agreed that they are being spent wisely.
