The point of difference between the minister and his supporters and those on this side of the house who are criticizing him is simply that we feel the money is not being spent wisely and that Canada is not getting value for her dollars in terms of defence. It should be made abundantly clear at this point that we feel the responsibility for this situation rests squarely upon the shoulders of the minister, the government and those at headquarters, and that it rests in no way upon the shoulders of the officers and men in the field and throughout the country who make up our defence forces. We know they are doing the very best job they possibly can under the defence system laid down for them, and with the resources and manpower at their command. For our part we feel that the inadequacy lies entirely in the framing of the defence policy which those officers and men are called upon to implement.
In his statement this afternoon, and in his statements during the period since he took over the department, the minister has consistently put forward the view that Canada's defence forces are adequate to Canada's needs and that they are well integrated with the defence requirements Canada may be called upon to meet under the Atlantic charter. Unfortunately we in this house are not in a position to comment on the latter point, because at no time has it been clearly stated-though we have frequently asked for this information-just what in fact is Canada's role in the Atlantic defence structure. So my remarks will be confined entirely to the question whether or not Canada's defence forces are adequately designed to meet our defence requirements, within the limited knowledge we have of our separate defence strategy; and my remarks and criticism will be based upon the minister's statements in that regard.
I should like to analyse a number of statements the minister has made over the past year or so, since February or March of 1948. In all those statements the emphasis has been upon the necessity for Canada to have defence forces able to defend our territory against attack from any quarter. I am sure all hon. members will appreciate that with our population it is going to be extremely difficult for us to defend our vast territory against attack from any quarter; but oddly enough that is the role the minister has laid upon our defence forces. Speaking in Montreal on February 10, 1948, and commenting upon the size and strength of the soviet armed forces, the Gazette of that date reports the minister as having used these words:
Mr. Claxton stressed that he was not suggesting that Russia was poised on the brink of war, but merely that she and her satellites have shown that

they are not ready to seek permanent security under law, and that as a consequence Canada "must ensure positive security under her own arms."
In his statement to the house this afternoon the minister supported that previous declaration, and also supported my contention that his emphasis is upon defence of our territory by our own forces. He said that our defence organization-referring entirely to Canada's domestic defence organization-must ensure the integrity of our territory. In other statements the minister has made he has given the impression that our recruiting policies and our armament and equipment policies all are proceeding satisfactorily and at a rate which will speedily ensure that our forces are of the size and nature, with sufficient equipment and armament, to fulfil the role he has laid upon them, namely that they should be capable of ensuring, virtually without outside support, the defence of our own territory from attack from any quarter.
That is the picture the minister has given; that is the role he has laid down and the impression he has left in the calculated statements he has made: that our defence forces are adequate for that role. Let us then examine the facts as they are disclosed in available returns, figures and information. When we examine the structure of our forces in the light of the minister's statements it becomes perfectly obvious that they are totally incapable of filling that role, if indeed they were ever designed or should ever be designed to do so, without some outside support or without being integrated into some defensive role within the structure of the North Atlantic alliance. Take the picture as to the strength of our services as shown in the annual report of the department. We find that the navy has an authorized strength of 10,375 all ranks, and that its present strength is 8,154. The army has an authorized strength of 26,329, and its present strength is 18,970. The air force has an authorized strength of 18,221 and a present strength of 14,552. So the total authorized strength of our permanent forces is 54,925. That is what is called the nucleus of our defence force, which is supposed to be adequate to defend our millions of square miles of territory, with thousands of miles of vulnerable sea coast and other thousands of miles of vulnerable northwestern approaches. This nucleus, which is supposed to be capable of defending all this territory, has an authorized strength of 54,925, and it falls short of even that pitiful authorized strength by more than 15 per cent, according to the last report issued by the department.
The whole picture the minister has given of our defence set-up is entirely misleading, in the first place because by ourselves, with

our limited population-and here I take direct issue with his statements-we cannot hope to defend our millions of square miles of vulnerable territory. In the second place they are misleading because the authorized objective set for the forces is short of attainment by over one-quarter. In other words, we are 15,000 short of even the objective of 54,925. It may be remarked that the picture I have presented so far leaves entirely out of account the reserve forces. It does. The picture would be redeemed in large part if in fact our reserve forces were up to strength, or if they were trained and equipped in such a way as to enable them to be rapidly expanded into an effective striking force in support of the permanent force. But the picture in that respect is far from encouraging, and falls short of the glowing rosy pictures the minister has painted. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that a country in Canada's position, with a small population and a vast territory to defend, in the first place must rely upon the Atlantic alliance to help defend our country.
But even then, as I have said, we have no clear picture of what our role is. We do not know. But taking the minister's statements as given to the house and to the members, even if we are fulfilling whatever role we are assigned in the Atlantic alliance, because of our limited population we must rely largely upon a reserve force which is capable of immediate expansion, of arming and equipping and of taking the field within the space of weeks or a month at the most from the outbreak of hostilities. The time factor was fully discussed this afternoon by the hon. member for Nanaimo. I do not need to go over that ground again in order to remind the committee or the minister that no longer in a future war, should a future war take place, shall we have time for a leisurely mobilization. If we are to play an effective role in defending our own territories, we must be able to put in the field an effective striking force within weeks or at the most a month of the time of the outbreak of hostilities. Is our reserve force capable of expansion in that way, to fill the role which that picture thrusts upon it? It certainly is not.
How do you know?

Because I happen to have looked into this matter of the reserve forces. As given in the published report of the Department of National Defence, at page 82, the strength of the reserve forces at the present time is as follows: for the navy, 3,272; for the army, 36,311; for the air force 1,427; total reserve forces of all three services, 41,010. If my hon. friend who asked me the question, or any other hon. member who
Supply-National Defence is interested, will take the trouble to consult with the commanding officers of any of our reserve units, he will find the answer to his question. Those officers are reluctantly compelled to say that their units would not be battleworthy for a period not of weeks or a month, but of months or a year. We therefore have not a reserve force capable of taking the field, under present conditions, within less than a year from the outbreak of hostilities.
Just as a matter of comparison, I should like to direct the attention of the committee to a few figures as to the size of the reserve army today as compared with what it was before the war. If you take any year from 1924-25 up to 1938-9, you will find that the size of the reserve army was substantially in excess of the reserve army of today. I give these figures by way of substantiating the statement that our reserve forces of today- and we know how long it took them to take the field in the last war and in the first world war-are even less prepared, less trained, less well equipped and less well manned, if I may use that expression, than they were at any period from 1925 to 1939.
Who says that?
The figures establish it.
The figures do not indicate anything of the kind; they do not indicate anything except the number of men on the strength.
Yes, but when one has knowledge of the state of training and equipment of the units in the years from 1925-1939, in comparison with what they are today,-
It does not show that at all.
-then the picture becomes clearer.
If one has that knowledge, it does become clear.

The minister's statements, which have been quoted in the chamber by others and by myself, as to the role of Canada's forces, as to the state of training, preparedness, equipment and recruitment, have been so misleading that I think this statement he has just made is equally misleading.
Withdraw.
Nonsense.

When one comes to the question of the other statements which have been made as to strengh and equipment, one sees an equally disturbing picture. Perhaps it would be interesting to the committee to have placed on the record some of the actual figures to which I refer, as to the strengths of
1696	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence the reserve forces in the period I have mentioned. To deal with the army, in 1924-25, 50,492. In 1930-31, 53,201; in 1935-36, 48,761; in 1938-39, 51,418. For the post-war period: in 1946-47, 37,657; in 1947-48, 33,591; and 1948-49, 36,311.
Then we come to some of the other statements of the minister with respect to the progress being made in bringing our forces up to strength; and we find that, when examined in the light of actuality, they have an equally disturbing eifect. I have here the answer which the minister made in the house on March 16, 1948. He was replying to a question asked by the former member for York South, with regard to recruitment for the army. As reported at page 2253 of Hansard, the minister's answer was:
... I can tell my hon. friend . . . that good progress is being made, and, in comparison with other countries where similar conditions obtain, the showing is encouraging. Men are being taken in at about the rates we want to have them for the army . . .
At that time the authorized strength of the army was 26,329; the actual strength was 15,409 or about 9,000 below the authorized strength. It will thus be seen that the minister's statements throughout, in the house and in the country, have been to the effect that Canada is well prepared, that her armed forces are well equipped, well trained and well manned to resist attack from whatever quarter it might come, and to defend our territory, of our own strength, against this attack.
Hon. members will recall that in March of last year the President of the United States made a very important and far-reaching statement on the subject of military preparedness, having to do with the personnel requirements of the United States armed forces in support of the efforts then being put forward to increase considerably the strength of those forces. In his speech before congress President Truman said-and I think this is the principle which should guide us in the design and equipping and manning of our forces-
We must be prepared to pay the price of peace or assuredly we shall pay the price of war.
In commenting on these remarks when speaking in Montreal in March of last year the Minister of National Defence said that the President's remarks were:
The beginning of the marshalling of force on the side of right which is essential if we are to preserve the way of life in which we believe.
On the basis of that statement, and the other statements which I have read, one would have assumed that Canada was playing a role comparable to that of the United States in proportion to our resources and to


our population. But if we compare the figures on the basis of population, and on the basis of the actual strength of the United States forces at that time, we find that Canada should have a permanent force of 150,000 if we are to play a role in proportion to that of the United States, as the statement of the minister would indicate we should. But the figures that have been given already indicate that the total authorized strength of our forces is 54,925. It seems to me that this has a definite bearing upon the role which Canada is called upon to play within the North Atlantic alliance. It may well be that under that alliance we have obligations of a different nature, or of a lesser proportion, than the military obligations assumed by the United States or the other parties to the alliance. If that is so, the country should be told. But it is misleading if statements are made which indicate that we are expected to bear, and are prepared to bear, a military role proportionate to that of the United States when in fact the authorized limit of our armed forces is only one-third of the present strength of the United States forces.
Our boys are worth three to one anyway.

I come next to the list of accomplishments given by the minister in the course of his remarks today. In many of those accomplishments there is cause for pride and satisfaction; but if they are analysed they are mainly with respect to improvements in the service standards, such things as the ration scale, the clothing, progress in provision of married quarters, and the start in aid of building, quarters for single men. The minister referred with pride to the shipbuilding program. When one analyses the accomplishment one finds that we have built one icebreaker. Then there is the aircraft program. We have placed orders for up-to-date jet fighters, but according to his statement our main accomplishment is in overhauling and modernizing machines.
The minister said that the training of the armed brigade group has been pressed on. That training in accordance with the reports on Exercise Eagle, which has been analysed in the light of what actually went on, has not been pressed on to the stage where the brigade group, the mobile permanent force group, is able to fulfil the role which the minister himself has laid down for it. The minister then went on to refer to the training in civilian defence. But if one analyses the statement on the basis of that statement alone it does not appear to have got much farther than the appointment of General Worthington. That is the record which the minister gave us this afternoon.

With respect to recruiting, the minister said that the campaign has been continued with the desired result in every respect, with the exception of the reserve army. If the results fall so far short of the authorized ceiling desired by the minister-and these were his words: they would produce the desired results -I suggest that he should immediately inform the country that in fact the glowing statements he has made as to the preparedness and equipment of our armed forces should be substantially modified because they are not yet ready to fulfil the role which he himself has outlined for them.
On the basis of these statements, these facts and figures, it is dangerously likely that the whole present defence policy of the government is not geared to the needs or the capabilities of the Canadian nation, and that the minister appears to be living in a world of unreality, not even he being aware of how far short our defence forces come of the goal that he himself has set, and in his own lack of knowledge or unwillingness to recognize that situation the country as a whole is unfortunately being misled. There is substantiation of this picture to be found in the words of the Mainguy report. At page 41 the commissioners report:
Several high authorities suggested that the navy is engaged in making too many bricks with too little straw. Most of the unsatisfactory conditions have been known to naval authorities for three years or more.
On page 42 they state:
iThe present actual complement of officers and men was stated by several witnesses to be inadequate for the existing commitments and tasks of the navy, if it is to concentrate on training, as it must do.
The significance of these statements, Mr. Chairman, is in the fact that the commissioners find that these conditions have been known to naval authorities for three years or more; and yet in the light of the inadequacies set forth in this report, many of which were known to naval authorities, the Minister of National Defence has consistently presented a picture of the armed forces, including the navy, which has come up to every expectation and which are thoroughly ready now to fulfil the role which he has set for them, which picture is obviously not consistent with the facts as shown in the figures issued by the department itself when compared with the statements made by the minister. In the light of these conditions it seems to me that the need becomes perfectly obvious for the setting up of a permanent defence committee of the Canadian House of Commons. This is a matter which in my experience has been pressed for every year since 1945. It is not a happy thing for any
Supply-National Defence hon. member to stand in the Canadian parliament and suggest, in fact state, that the Canadian services are not ready to fulfil the role which has been set for them as their task in defending this country. The statements I have made have been made on the basis of an analysis of the facts and figures given by the minister and his department, in comparison with the statements made by the same minister with respect to the role of those forces.
I realize that the inner details concerning these facts and figures are not fully known to me or any other member on this side of the house-and I doubt if they are fully known to any member on the other side, because we have not been given the opportunity to become fully acquainted with all the details and ramifications of the defence role of our forces. Particularly, we have not been told what is Canada's role within the structure of the North Atlantic treaty.
So that what I have been saying tonight has been said seriously, on the basis of the best information I have been able to acquire 

the information given by the department itself. If there are gaps in it, if there are injustices or apparent injustices to Canada's armed forces, the reason for those injustices is the incomplete knowledge or the gaps in the knowledge available to myself and other members of the house.
The desire of all members is to assist the department in so far as we can in building forces equipped to fulfil the role set for them, and also in acquainting the country and our constituents with the needs of Canada's defence forces in order that we may encourage support for those services, in order that we may within the limits of our responsibility and our opportunities encourage even recruiting, if need be. But with the lack of information we are totally unqualified to fulfil that which I suggest with respect is the perfectly proper role for any member of parliament in face of the very serious world situation with which we are confronted today.
I make these few remarks in support of a renewed plea for the setting up of a national defence committee of the Canadian House of Commons, and conclude by reminding the committee that this request was made in 1945. The then minister of national defence said he entirely agreed that it was a reasonable request, and said the same thing again in 1946, when the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra, and the hon. member for Nanaimo-supported on each occasion by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, the leader of the C.C.F.-made the request.
In 1946 the then prime minister said he felt, too, that it was a reasonable request, a
1698	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence desirable thing and in the best interests of the defence of the country that such a committee be set up. May I read the words of Mr. Mackenzie King as they appear in Hansard for March 29, 1946:
I think the suggestion of my hon. friend is a very good one-
Referring to the suggestion put forward on that occasion by the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra-
-and, as the Minister of National Defence has just said, it is one that he is prepared to consider sympathetically.
Then, after pointing out that at that particular moment, when a number of special committees were being set up, it would be difficult to constitute such a committee on national defence, the Prime Minister concluded with these words, as they appear at page 406 of Hansard:
I think my hon. friend's suggestion of that particular committee is a very good one.
The then prime minister's remarks concerning the necessity for a committee, and the desirability of informing all members of the house and all citizens of the country as to the requirements of Canada's defence forces, and as to the way in which they can best serve to fulfil those requirements, have not lost force since that date. In fact, in view of the world situation of today-and even in spite of the misgivings we have as to the adequacy of the minister's policy-we are prepared to support these estimates amounting to $383 million. I believe the necessity for that committee is vastly greater today than it was in 1946 when the then prime minister said he considered it a very good idea. I hope the minister will give his consent finally to the setting up of such a committee.

Mr. Chairman, probably
it would meet the convenience of the committee if I were to deal with some of the points raised by hon. members in their very helpful remarks. If the hon. member for Kamloops will pardon me, however, I shall not endeavour to correct every inaccuracy he has been uttering in the course of his remarks. But I should just like to say that his interpretation of the statements to which he has referred is so far away from any natural and proper interpretation that the words will bear, that I do not think it is necessary for me to follow him through that course.
However, I should like to deal with some of the express questions or points raised by hon. members and express appreciation to them of everything they have said of a helpful nature. First, turning to the question raised by the hon. member for Calgary East,


and referred to again by the hon. member for Kamloops, as to our commitments in the North Atlantic treaty. It is perfectly clear that we have no commitments whatever under the North Atlantic treaty. The organization under the treaty has just been set up. The regional groups have been organized and the appropriate officers and representatives of the various governments concerned are considering what should be the various strategical plans and requirements.
This is expressly dealt with in paragraph 12 of the statement I gave, in which I said:
It is still too early to spell out the consequences of the pact in terms of men and dollars.
And that is said after I have described the organizational work up to this present time.
When shall we know our commitments under that treaty?

Well, first of all, there will be no commitments except with the consent of the government of Canada; and, secondly, there will be no commitments until the strategical considerations to which I have just now referred, and to which I referred in greater length before, have been given attention.
About when would that be?

I have no means of estimating a date. It depends largely upon the work of people outside the Canadian government and forces. For example, in the western European group, there are five nations as well as Canada and the United States as observers. They will be meeting and working things out. Then there will be consultations between the different groups, anjl ultimately clearance both by the standing group, the defence committee and the council. So that while this operation is being pressed forward with all speed, it will of necessity take some time.
With regard to another point raised by the hon. member for Calgary East, and referred to by others, I should like to make it perfectly plain again-and I want to state it as definitely as I can-that we have been getting recruits since January 1, 1948, and before that, at the rate we required, at the planned rate, for the active navy, the army and the air force, and for the navy reserve and the air force auxiliary. If we got recruits at a faster rate it would be necessary to have increased training establishments and increased capital equipment, neither of which would be justified by our concept of the strategical situation.
What about the army reserve?

I dealt with that before. We now have some 39,000 men in the army reserve, and I should like to see about

another 10,000 there. We have been doing everything we can to support the commands and to give national direction to campaigns to that end. In that connection the hon. member for Calgary East paid a well merited tribute to the officers and men of the reserve who have done a magnificent job. However, he referred to the recruiting campaigns as being a flop. In January, 1948, we had in the reserve forces of Canada a strength of 36,173; in September, 1949, it was 45,123.
Again I do not like making comparisons with other countries because they are so liable to be inaccurate and misleading and one must take into account all factors; but with regard to the strength of our reserve forces, navy, army and air, I want to say that they are greater in proportion to population than any country in the British commonwealth and considerably greater than the corresponding forces in Great Britain. That is nothing to be thankful for, but it does indicate that we are tackling this problem and securing a response relative to the present situation within three or four years of the end of a war, at a time of full employment and when our young men are interested in other things, which I think is encouraging, all things being considered.
The situation is satisfactory with respect to everything except the reserve army and I think it is encouraging in that connection. I know the position of the commanding officers of the reserve army because I was in the reserve for a time myself. They do have a difficult time when there is not an adequate number of men. I have never suggested for one second, as was said by one hon. member, that we do not want men in the reserve army. Of course we do. The hon. member was good enough to suggest that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and I should make an appeal for recruits, bringing home the need. We have both done that repeatedly. The Prime Minister has shown the utmost interest in the work of all the armed forces.
The suggestion made with regard to armouries is well founded. There is nothing I should like more than to be able to begin the construction of armouries wherever they are needed across Canada, but it is a question, first, of labour, then materials and then money. The hon. member suggested that we should try to procure temporary accommodation by the use of existing buildings. That is a most useful suggestion. In fact we are already doing it. Since 1939, in the last ten years, we have increased the floor space of armouries for the reserve army by 70 per cent. That is a substantial increase, being nearly double, but still more is needed because of the great quantities of equipment which modern reserve armies have.
Supply-National Defence
We are continuing the practice of increasing accommodation wherever we can and we have let a contract for the construction of the first new armoury for a major unit at Sault Ste. Marie. The cost of this indicates that here again real money is required. The contract is for $850,000 for an armoury to accommodate a single unit.
The hon. member was good enough to say that training had been improved and there was a considerable increase in numbers, and of course it is most satisfactory to hear him say that, because he has been in both the reserve and the active forces. The hon. member said the air force equipment situation was not good, but here we must be realistic. We must understand what modern defence forces mean.
At the present time we are at work on the XC-100, a twin-jet all-weather fighter. If that plane is a success when it is tested it will be two or three years in advance of any plane of its type anywhere. We are at work on the construction of the F-86 which is as far as we know the fastest plane there is. I was asked by one hon. member how long it will take to produce these. We are working at a planned rate to produce these planes, not as fast as possible because we do not expect war within a year, but at a rate which will provide an economical flow from the factory where they are produced.
If I could show hon. members the schedules of production for planes in countries much larger than ours they would be astonished at how they differ from wartime rates. It is simply because countries have not the means to rearm at the rate they would like. It is interesting to note that in one of his fine statements on defence when speaking about the navy in the United States General Bradley said that the United States, with all its great wealth and resources, the richest country on earth, had to choose the things that would come first, had to work on priorities, because they did not have all the money they wanted for defence. Of course that is well known, and we are in the same position.
If any hon. member thinks that our armed forces are too small, that we should recruit faster, let him realize that that means $2,600 per year for each man taken on, and for each subsequent year until the man goes out of the army.
Is that active or reserve?

Active, and the figure is approximately the same for each of the three services. That does not include any overhead. If you want more in the way of equipment, it must be paid for. What is

Supply-National Defence almost more important, new equipment involves continuing commitments for maintenance, repairs and modifications. Modifications are the bugbear of all defence planners, particularly at a time of rapid change and development. Almost every piece of equipment seems to be subject to modifications before it is even delivered.
The hon. member for Melfort remarked that this year we were spending only five per cent of the defence dollar on research whereas last year we spent six per cent. The percentages given in that table are in round figures. The actual amounts are given in vote 251 of the estimates. The figure for 1948-49 was $19,700,000 for defence research, and the figure for 1949-50 is $21 million. Therefore, while the actual percentage shows a decrease, the actual amount has increased because of the fact that the over-all defence appropriation, when granted by parliament, will be 50 per cent over what it was last year. There is an increase in every single item in the table. We are cognizant of the need for keeping up with defence research. It is an important aspect of defence policy. There again our work is closely related with that of friendly nations along the lines of the hon. member's suggestion. Our working arrangements with the United States and the United Kingdom are just as close as they could be in all aspects of the matter.
References were also made to the shortages of kit. described in the Mainguy report. The shortages, as they have been reported to me, occurred between November, 1948, and June, 1949, and they applied to certain sizes of caps, collars, shirts, shoes, two types of trousers, underwear and vests. They did not extend to major items of clothing, and they were in certain sizes only. It is difficult to plan the purchase of clothing so as to keep on hand an adequate supply of all sizes at all times unless very large stocks are maintained.
Are the shortages you refer to at Esquimalt, or the alarming shortages which were referred to as existing at headquarters?
The shortages at Esquimalt; the other is the same question.
What about the situation in the army and the air force?

If I may finish my answer on this matter, I will come to that. As to what caused the shortages, it was due, largely but not entirely, to the navy getting recruits faster than they had planned or expected. It was due largely to that, but also to the fact that their methods of stock-keeping, unlike those in effect in the army and air force, were not as modern and up to date as they should have been; consequently they


did not provide for easy advance planning. That is being changed. The shortages have been overcome now and the matter has been cleared up.
As to the time that it takes to obtain clothing, where the cloth has to be woven' as is usually the case with uniforms, delivery takes over a year from the time of placing the order. Therefore planning must be related to the flow of recruits and discharges, and if we get more recruits and have fewer discharges than we expect, we are likely to run short at a time of rapid build-up.
Dealing with the army and the air force, I am informed that apart from occasional shortages of certain sizes, particularly unusual ones, there is no shortage, and that further we are gradually building up some stocks to meet future needs. The new summer uniform is in general issue now, and the blue uniform will come into general issue towards the latter part of 1950.
The hon. member for Churchill was good enough to refer to the Royal Military College and our efforts to re-establish the college on a sound footing. As hon. members know, he is one of two men in the house-the Minister of Mines and Resources is the other

who are ex-cadets of that famous institution. I must say that the progress made in securing close co-operation with respect to the training of officers for the navy, army and air force is encouraging in view of the fact that the college was only opened again in September, 1948.
The hon. member for Calgary East referred to the question of civil defence. Here we have had a difficult dedision of timing to make. We could very easily proceed to set up local civil defence organizations in every community right across Canada. There is no doubt that local communities would cooperate in that respect, and that work could be done. I may be wrong but my belief, based on such experience as I have had with organization, is that if local organizations were set up in every part of Canada and there was nothing for them to do except carry on for any considerable period the kind of training that civil defence groups would, then the men and women who would devote their spare time to this activity would soon cease to be interested in it, and would not be on hand should an emergency arise. The whole job of organization would have to be done over again. That is the view on which we have acted.
That does not mean, however, that that view is going to remain constant. With the progress in other directions which I expect there will be, we are working towards the organization of civil defence based first of all

on all the government departments concerned with the question, and then the provinces, because almost all matters that have to do with civil defence have provincial aspects. Some of them are exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and in many matters the municipalities are mainly concerned. General Worthington has studied what is now being done in other countries as well as what was done during the last war. He has also interviewed the provinces. We have had a planning committee at Ottawa with representatives of the government departments concerned, and the matter has reached the stage where we could very speedily set up a plan and put it into effect. It would be a matter of hours to do that. We can now move on to the next stage of getting it developed at various levels so that we shall have a skeleton organization on which to build a civil defence body in every part of the country to meet any need.
While I am on my feet I should like to say a word to make clear one thing I think is important. In paragraph 29 of my statement concerning Canada's defence program, I referred to the development of radar; and I should like to quote the passage:
To meet attack by air requires jet interceptors and anti-aircraft guns with the necessary radar equipment and communications system, backed by a relatively small but highly trained, efficient and mobile force of ground troops. The territory of Canada is so vast that it is obviously impracticable to construct a chain or grid of radar warning stations similar in density and consequent effectiveness to the installations during the last war in the smaller areas of Britain or Germany; nevertheless an early warning system to cover certain vital approaches and areas is being developed.
That paragraph should be read as it appears. It would be beyond the economic and industrial resources of Canada to provide a radar defence system or an anti-aircraft defence system such as Britain had during the second world war. Moreover it would involve our country in static defence to a degree which would virtually paralyse any offensive effort; and even then it would not be one hundred per cent effective. Hon. members know, because many were there, that Britain was bombed despite radar and interceptor defences of the kind I have mentioned. In fact perhaps only ten per cent of the aircraft on bombing raids were knocked down. This is a field in which we must have knowledge of all developments and must be prepared to do what we can to defend vital and vulnerable points, and in which we must begin the development of what is considered a proper level of defence; but I hope no one will think for a second that we are going to put a string of radar stations over the North pole or anything of the sort. We are not. We could not
Supply-National Defence do that, and it would not be the right way to spend our defence dollars.
Once again, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that in this field it would be interesting indeed to hear suggestions that our forces are too small or too large, that the relative proportion as between the three services is not correct, or that we are spending too much on personnel or on equipment and properties. But such suggestions have not been made during this discussion, as far as I know. The fact is that we can only increase the strength of our armed forces today by spending more money. We can only increase the equipment or build more properties by spending more money. The question then is: How much money do the Canadian people feel that the risks involved require us to spend? Obviously if we believed that within a year there would be a war involving us and the whole world, this is not the kind of appropriation we would be seeking. We would not be spending time discussing hundreds of millions. I am afraid it would go into billions, and many of them. All defence planning depends of necessity upon the calculation of risk and the estimation of forces, both those of any prospective enemy and those of any prospective friends. The next step is to spend the money made available out of the national budget in the most intelligent way to meet the needs as economically as we can.
That is a task which I can assure the committee is proving difficult in every country, because there are so many uncertain factors in the whole situation. But it is a task in which we have had the advantage of good advice from very competent officers, and also of discussion and consultation with our friends in other countries.
As a final word, the hon. member referred to high overhead; and I must say I often feel that the overhead, the number of men we have on the staff, seems very large indeed. It is not much consolation, either, to find that my opposite numbers in Britain and the United States are similarly concerned; but the fact is that this has become an exceedingly complicated and technical business requiring very considerable numbers of experienced, highly trained and well educated staff, both officers and men. Then again in this field, which involves so much in the way of co-operation between the services and also between one country and another, we have a great many inter-service and international committees which require considerable groups of personnel. However, in making comparisons with the forces of other countries, I do not think we are in any respect worse off, with regard to either the overhead or the proportion of civilians. But it is a matter that requires constant attention and

Supply-National Defence that I can assure you is receiving the attention of the chiefs of staff, the deputy minister and myself.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, during the course of my remarks this afternoon I stressed as emphatically as I could that I did not think sufficient emphasis was being placed on the air force. Obviously, if I did not make it clear, the inference was that I thought a larger proportion of money was being spent on the other services. Therefore I was surprised to hear the statement made by the minister just now. My feeling that greater emphasis should be placed upon the air force was one of the main reasons why I asked for the setting up of a committee to investigate this whole question of defence policy.
